Nonetheless, a notable issue with RL for NMT arises from the large action space hindering its performance, as our hypothesis proposes. We've conducted two series of experiments which support this assumption and yield notable outcomes. Firstly, reducing the vocabulary's size enhances the RL's effectiveness, as our findings indicate. Furthermore, a notable improvement can be observed when the action space is reduced without changing the vocabulary, as validated by multiple metrics including BLEU scores, semantic similarity and human assessment. Our research discovered that initializing the final fully connected layer with a layer that generalizes action similarities resulted in substantial RL performance gains, averaging 1.5 BLEU points improvement.

A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that relies on real-world depth camera data rather than simulation or fiducial markers. Our system leverages machine learning to automatically develop and utilize real-world models for identifying and positioning the end-effector, predicting object rotation, and pinpointing critical points in a single image frame. A mathematical transformation and a keypoint-matching algorithm allow us to accurately estimate end-effector pose based on rotation and keypoint data. Enhanced system robustness is achieved through a combination of advanced algorithms, including the iterative closest point method, multi-frame processing, filtering, and outlier detection. Results show our method's calibration and pose estimation capabilities can be as precise as sub-centimeters and sub-degrees with minimal and unseen test poses; we have also found that incorporating data from just one optimal pose yields comparable accuracy.

This study introduces two key concepts, quasi-finitely separating maps and quasiapproximate identities, which form the basis for the definitions of QFS-spaces and quasicontinuous maps. Building upon these definitions, various properties and characteristics of QFS-spaces are investigated. Key findings include: Firstly, any QFS-space is inherently a quasicontinuous space; secondly, closed subspaces, as well as quasicontinuous projection spaces, derived from QFS-spaces are themselves QFS-spaces; thirdly, continuous retracts of QFS-spaces possess the same characteristic and specific types of QFS-space retracts can be constructed; lastly, upper power spaces of continuous QFS-spaces correspond to FS-spaces.

The rise of partisanship seems to be rising across various metrics including voter behavior and online engagement. Research into the Web's influence on polarization has produced several key findings in the past. To build on existing research and gain deeper insights, we've studied browsing habits of thousands of users along with their online interactions with news sources. Our results reveal that users' online exposure to news sources follows distinct ideological patterns where they consistently spend more time browsing news aligned with their own viewpoint. Moreover, we've identified clear partisan groups within the broader online population based on shared browsing habits. Ultimately, we examined the impact of user decision-making on online polarization, and we've uncovered substantial evidence indicating users' deliberate actions can contribute significantly to the amplification of partisan divisions.

We examine the Lehnert and Schweitzer proof that the word problem for Thompson's group V has a non-context-free property. We further prove this word problem to be equivalent to the complement of a combined cyclic variant of several context-free languages, and for some of its generators, the combined cyclic variant of four deterministic context-free languages is sufficient. This relationship reveals that the time complexity of solving V's word problem deterministically is no more than quadratically scaling with input size.

The study of open quantum systems under periodic driving forces is highly captivating 
because, in most cases, they achieve a non-equilibrium steady state, which is
marked by a constant current. In this study, we examine discrete time-driven
dynamics in the laboratory using a single photon system that is linked to its surroundings.
Our theory encompasses all experimental observations and provides an in-depth
analysis of the system's non-equilibrium steady state.
Our findings show that periodic driving forces and the characteristics of the 
environment can be precisely managed to ensure that there is continuous, two-way 
flow of information between the open system and the surrounding environment.

We explore how several established recurrent operators including curvature, Ricci, Jacobi, shape, and Weyl operators contribute substantially to biharmonic hypersurfaces being minimal within the Euclidean space.

A rational number p/q represents the basis of a numbering system. Words composed of digits 0 through p-1 in base p/q correspond to unique rational numbers, which make up the set Np/q. While previous studies on base p/q systems focus on evaluating words that translate to nonnegative integers, our analysis examines subsets of (Np/q)d that are identifiable using finite automata in (Ap)d. Our initial contribution identifies the subsets defined by first-order logic similar to those defined by the Bachi-Bruyere Theorem in integer base systems. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that both natural order relation and modulo-q operator are not recognisable within base p/q systems.

Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a simple QCD axion sector to the Standard Model effectively explains multiple phenomena including neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry. In doing so, it also resolves issues with strong CP problems and stabilizes the electroweak vacuum while fitting within observational limits of Higgs inflation. The model, referred to as $a\nu$MSM, undergoes a detailed analysis to examine the nature of dark matter within this framework. The presence of an inflection point within Higgs inflation is found not to significantly impact dark matter composition, and thus the model instead presents a multicomponent DM system involving axions and sterile neutrinos. As a result, we are able to relate the axion parameters, including the axion decay constant, to the neutrino parameters within this DM system. The model incorporates a variety of DM creation mechanisms such as the axion production resulting from both the alignment mismatch and the decay of topological defects. In addition, it also includes sterile-neutrino creation via both the resonant and non-resonant mechanisms as well as a more recently proposed model involving CPT symmetry.

Between October 2019 and April 2020, the LAMOST performed a unique observational study using four $K$2 plates. This study, which involved low- and medium-resolution spectroscopic surveys, gathered a significant amount of data. The low-resolution spectroscopic survey yielded around 767,000 spectra after 25 nights of 46.6 hours of exposures and a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 70% of its spectra. The medium-resolution spectroscopic survey took 177 exposures and around 49.1 hours over 27 nights to collect around 478,000 spectra. The data showed a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 50% of its spectra. To estimate the stellar parameters and radial velocities, the LAMOST research team utilized several different methods such as LASP, DD-Payne, and SLAM. These estimations demonstrated good agreement and were consistent with those of the APOGEE study. By analyzing the $Gaia$ DR2 data, the LAMOST research team corrected for radial velocity zero points on a per exposure basis, showing good alignment with the APOGEE study. To estimate stellar masses, the LAMOST research team utilized stellar parameters and multi-band magnitudes in combination with distances and extinction values. Ultimately, the LAMOST research team constructed a binary catalog

In image recognition, distinct forms of visual cues, namely edges and textures, contribute uniquely to the overall understanding. While edges convey crucial information about a shape's form, textures reveal details about regional appearance. Current Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) applications often excel at extracting texture information but tend to produce vague boundary definitions. Expert medical analysts, for instance, primarily utilize organ edges when performing manual segmentations. Influenced by these observations, this study proposes Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs), an easily integrable module that complements standard encoder-decoder networks, capable of processing edge and texture information simultaneously. By prioritizing edge extraction and incorporating an auxiliary supervision, the EG-CNN module refines its output and merges it with original network predictions. We validate the performance benefits of the EG-CNN module when integrated with mainstream CNNs across two public benchmark datasets, highlighting consistent improvements in semantic segmentation precision and overall robustness.

MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to pseudocode and formal specifications of the consistency guarantees they provide. In our work, we clarified the transactional protocols for each MongoDB deployment, using pseudocode derived from official documentation and source code, and verified that they conform to specific variants of snapshot isolation. Our approach also enables efficient checking of the consistency guarantees that MongoDB transactions provide.

Using the elementary symmetric function basis, we re-express the chromatic symmetric functions of Dyck paths with a bounce number of three via a combinatorial interpretation related to the inverse of the Kostka matrix from Egecioglu-Remmel (1990). This analysis shows the positivity of specific coefficients and confirms $e$-positivity for an expanded class of these functions, beyond a particular instance explored in Cho-Huh (2019).

We begin by defining a task for few-shot continual learning and propose a theory to explain how executive function works through a self-updating decision-making system that reprocesses perception data through a review of past experiences in order to minimize prediction errors. This idea becomes practical due to the incorporation of a memory mechanism and a pre-trained neural network that is predisposed to follow rules of effective learning and adapts to optimize its chances of long-term success. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our model of executive function can facilitate the development of hypothesis testing as an internal reasoning process and might provide insight into observed abilities of human learning and the organization of the human brain.

The success of medical image analysis using machine learning largely relies on high-quality datasets.  However, when these datasets contain biases, the models can learn them, compromising their ability to generalize and produce reliable results.  While research exists on developing unbiased models, the problem lies in identifying and mitigating the inherent biases present in medical image datasets.  In an effort to address this issue, we first establish a metric to quantify data intrinsic bias and propose a new framework for detecting biases in medical image datasets.  Our proposed framework, comprising of two primary components, namely KlotskiNet and Bias Discriminant Direction Analysis, aims to identify and quantify the inherent biases present in medical image datasets.  Our experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework in accurately identifying biases.

Research on intricate systems from the human brain to social connections has uncovered a higher-level structure that can be characterized through aggregates of interconnected triangles. To uncover these concealed geometric patterns, researchers are using topological methods and advanced graph theory to analyze and study dynamic processes occurring within these complex networks. This study leverages a recently developed model for triangle-based network assembly, where nanoscale triangular structures undergo spin reversal due to magnetic forces between connected nodes, fostering geometric frustration that drives novel phenomena in condensed matter physics. By manipulating the model's parameters, researchers observe how the shift from pair-based to triangular interactions affects ordering patterns, influencing the shape of resulting hysteresis loops. Moreover, the associated noise exhibited robust indicators of self-organization criticality, an emergent property solely induced by the intricate geometry of the network and not any inherent disorder.

We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and counteract gravity is about 70 Watts per square meter, plus or minus 14 Watts. Notably, this is similar to the findings of other researchers using data from different spacecraft and covering a longer time period, but with a key difference: the solar wind energy distributions were more symmetrical and followed a specific distribution pattern during these close encounters, unlike the more irregular and skewed patterns seen during the more typical intervals studied by those other researchers.

Thanks to speech-emotion recognition technology, computers can engage with people on a more emotional level. Nonetheless, the accuracy of speech-emotion recognition in real-world situations remains an area of improvement. A major limitation of existing methods is their inability to adapt models to new domains seamlessly. In response, researchers have developed innovative domain adaptation techniques that transfer knowledge across domains, yielding significant improvements. While these advancements are promising, there is still room for growth in adapting models to real-time, live data scenarios. A deep reinforcement learning-based strategy is presented here to adapt a pre-trained model in real-time while interacting with its environment. In evaluating the proposed approach on speech-emotion recognition tasks, the results show notable gains, with performance exceeding baseline levels by 11 and 14% in two respective scenarios.

We present an investigation of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ (BFTO), a four-layer Aurivillius compound, under the influence of high hydrostatic pressure.  Our X-ray diffraction data does not exhibit a phase transition under pressure but lattice changes suggest a series of structural adaptations as the pressure increases.  Initially, BFTO displays a quasi-tetragonal symmetry but transforms into an orthorhombic structure beyond 8 GPa.  Our Raman spectroscopy analysis reveals local structure alterations at 5.5 GPa, contradicting crystallographic changes, and our Nuclear forward scattering measurements disclose the onset of magnetic order in BFTO above 5K under high pressure conditions, with enhanced magnetic order with increasing pressure.  Conversely, NFS at 6.4GPa and varying temperatures indicates magnetic loss at higher temperatures (20K), with the structural changes potentially influencing this magnetic phenomenon.

Hybrid methods for continuous shortest path problems on a manifold hold significant potential, particularly in flight planning. To test these algorithms, a straightforward hybrid approach was created and its performance was evaluated against conventional routing. The evaluation was conducted using an automated dataset that simulates real-world flight patterns by calculating shortest paths to flight targets, with the aim of understanding how graph density affects the complexity of computed paths. A correlation was found between flight path difficulty and graph density, leading to the conclusion that flight targets density influences flight profiles. Furthermore, the research explored how introducing a secondary search space can streamline computed paths, although actual flight decisions may not always follow this optimal strategy.

Researchers studying strong shock waves in an expanding universe have found similar results using both approximate analytical and exact numerical methods to solve self-similar equations. When the adiabatic index lies between one and approximately 1.16, these solutions consistently occupy all space without gaps, showing close alignment with each other. As the index surpasses this threshold, pressure drops to zero at a finite distance from the origin, and in both scenarios, a spherical void forms. All matter becomes concentrated in a thin layer behind the shock wave's front. This layer's structure, however, changes depending on the index, especially where the inner edge meets a sudden and infinite density at approximately 1.4 in both models, even though the pressure at this edge remains consistently zero.

Using 13 TeV proton-proton collision data, specifically 1.7 inverse femtobarns of luminosity collected by the LHCb detector, the shape of the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^+\nu_{\mu}$ differential decay rate is determined as a function of hadron recoil. This rate is reconstructed via the $D_s^{-}$ decay sequence into $K^-K^+\pi^-$, following $D_s^{*-}$ decay into $D_s^{-}\gamma$. The resulting rate is initially isolated from background but further refined after subtracting an incorrectly combined signal from $D_s^{-}\bar{D_s^{-}}$ pairs. Both samples exhibit similar $\gamma$ mass distributions. The final, more precise result from the $B_s^0$ decays matches the initial, less accurate data.

A recent paper provides an analysis of advancements made in categorizing monodromy-free Schrödinger operators with rational potential properties. A specific subset of potential properties is studied which comprise generalized Hermite polynomials, constructed through the use of Wronskians from standard Hermite polynomials, often seen in mathematical physics and random matrix theories. This class of quadratic potentials displays oscillatory behavior near the origin and we establish an explicit condition to determine non-singularity, including an assessment of localization with respect to polynomial index and the location of zeros within the complex plane. Furthermore, one-dimensional Supersymmetric Quantum Mechanics reveals that non-singular potentials arise from combining the harmonic oscillator with polynomial versions of Heisenberg's ladder operators, effectively encapsulating generalized Hermite polynomials through periodic closure, leading to solutions to the Painlevé IV equation and revealing a connection between Schrödinger operator discrete spectra and the monodromy-free property.

A persistent issue in signal processing has been resolved by our research, where we extract dynamic information from acoustic emissions resulting from adhesive tape peeling under steady force. Through phase space reconstruction, our findings reveal the deterministic chaotic nature of these dynamics by confirming the existence of a correlation dimension and a positive Lyapunov exponent at specific traction velocities. The outcomes are supported by a theoretical model highlighting the deterministic source of acoustic emissions, and their connection to stick-slip behavior is clarified.

In epitaxial InAs/Al structures, our experimental analysis reveals the stochastic behavior of planar Josephson junctions and SQUIDs as temperature varies, exhibiting a crossover between macroscopic quantum tunneling and phase diffusion. The threshold temperature for this phase transition, T*, can be manipulated by adjusting a gate. The observed switching probability distributions are in line with minimal capacitance and moderate resistance, causing the switching current to be only a small portion of the critical current. Furthermore, synchronization between two JJs can cause a disparity in the switching current, where the difference in this current and the charging energy can be used to test for minimal dissipation.

The Yang-Mills-aether theory is analyzed to understand the implications of introducing non-abelian aether-like terms that violate Lorentz symmetry, specifically within thermal quantum field theory. By incorporating temperature effects and spatial compactification via Thermofield Dynamics, corrections to the non-abelian Stefan-Boltzmann law and non-abelian Casimir energy and pressure are calculated for both zero and finite temperatures.

This research develops a method for estimating the expected cost of hedging European options through the delta-hedging process, resulting in a computationally efficient formula that accounts for option prices and the behavior of delta processes. Initially, a standard unit hedging cost is established and subsequently, the total hedging cost is determined as the product of this unit cost, stock price, a supply curve factor, and the square of the number of options. Consequently, this formulation enables faster computation of expected hedging costs than alternative Monte Carlo methods. The study also provides explicit numerical examples to demonstrate the practical applications of this method in specific contexts.

By applying variational techniques, we develop a limiting model for a set of functionals subject to linear differential constraints. This framework models the energy of a heterogeneous material with a high-contrast composite structure at a microscopic scale, comprising a periodically perforated matrix filled with a dissimilar substance. Our key finding involves analyzing the $\Gamma$-convergence as the material periodicity diminishes, demonstrating that the limit functional comprises two components: the stored energy within the matrix, and the stored energy within the fillings. To overcome the coercivity issue inherent in the material structure, we employ two-scale convergence methods, while novel results are established for addressing the linear differential constraints via existence proofs for potentials and constraint-preserving extension operators.

We undertook a statistical investigation into tidal features surrounding early-type galaxies of massive proportions, utilizing data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program. Our analysis revealed that roughly 28 percent of 2649 galaxies, selected due to their mass greater than $10^{11}M_{\odot}$ and within a redshift range of 0.05-0.15, exhibited distinct tidal features exceeding one percent flux fraction. Observations indicated an exponential decline in the number of galaxies as tidal features became more pronounced. Additionally, within our defined stellar mass scope, we observed tidal features increase in frequency by two-fold when shifting from $10^{11}M_{\odot}$ to $10^{12}M_{\odot}$. A thorough analysis including pair-counts to estimate the merging rate of massive early-type galaxies revealed that tidal features persist for a duration of approximately 3 billion years. This outcome was found to align with findings from prior studies.

A higher education system or similar opportunities can drive social mobility across generations by allowing individuals to rise above their family's economic status. To examine this dynamic in societies with social mobility limitations, a new model allocates opportunities to maximize the benefits they provide to current and future generations. Our model reveals that, in order to maximize long-term payoffs, it's beneficial to give priority to lower socioeconomically situated individuals who have greater potential to rise to better socioeconomical standings. The result can lead to socioeconomic affirmative action. The duration and intensity of this practice vary depending on specific conditions. The proposed model also offers ways to manipulate these conditions to either eliminate or ensure affirmative action in optimal opportunities allocations.

The combination of chirped pulse amplification and nonlinear optical systems has been the foundation for significant progress in numerous sectors, including semiconductors, communications, biology, defense, and national security. However, accurately modeling these laser systems using CPA and NLO is a complex task due to their interconnected linear and nonlinear processes, and the high variability in available modeling frameworks. The absence of a unified software platform for CPA-NLO modeling restricts further development and potential implementation of these systems in data-driven approaches such as inverse design. We introduce a modular software model that encompasses various amplifier configurations and nonlinear techniques, and demonstrates its capabilities through the example of a high-average-power laser system capable of 375-W continuous output and 800-fs short pulses. This modular design enables easy integration of new configurations and facilitates real-time data analysis for the optimization and control of complex laser systems.

It is proven that for each $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$ and $x_1,\ldots,x_n \in L_p(\mu)$ where the largest absolute value among them does not exceed $K$, there exist vectors $y_1,\ldots,y_n \in \ell_p^d$ such that the dimension $d$ is approximately $K^{4p}\varepsilon^{-4}(n + n^2 \log n)$, and for all $i,j \in \{1,\ldots,n\}$, $\big\||x_i - x_j\| - \|y_i - y_j\|\big\| \le \varepsilon$, $\big||x_i| - |y_i|\big\| \le \varepsilon$, and $\big||x_i|x_j| - |y_i||y_j||\big\| \le \varepsilon$, under the assumption that $\mu$ is a Borel measure on a metric space $(S,d)$ and $\|x_i\|$ denotes the $\mu$-integral of the function with value $d(x_i,x)$. In 2015, CERN introduced "Emittance Scans," a new fast luminosity separation scanning method at the Large Hadron Collider. These scans were consistently carried out during physics production runs, utilizing full-intensity beams at the CMS experiment's interaction point. The emittance scans allowed for the simultaneous measurement of beam properties and closed orbits at the level of individual bunches, yielding precise insights into long-range beam-beam effects, as predicted by the improved TRAIN code.

This paper explores the optimization challenges in multi-agent systems that involve agents behaving maliciously, which leads to a misdirection away from optimal solutions through the spread of false information and significant communication costs. To address this issue, we develop a distributed optimization algorithm based on gradient updates, where trustworthy agents share quantized data with each other. Theoretical proof of solution convergence near the optimal solution is provided, along with the effects of communication constraints and malicious behavior on solution accuracy. This is further illustrated through numerical experiments presented in the study.

The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated and highly sensitive experiments that observe the sky across various frequencies with thousands of polarisation-sensitive detectors. As such experiments become increasingly sensitive, they are susceptible to being limited by instrumental systematic effects when trying to fully utilise their data. This paper presents a Python tool,'s4cmb', which generates simulated raw data streams in the time domain for contemporary cosmic microwave background experiments based on bolometric technology. The package also incorporates realistic instrumental systematic effects into the simulated data, with the goal of helping researchers assess the impact of such effects on actual data, informing future instrument design, and making simulated data sets more realistic for the development of accurate data analysis techniques.

In the task of arranging unordered words into a meaningful order, prior approaches rely on either linear models or neural networks, without examining the role of pre-trained language models, including why they would be beneficial. Utilizing BART as an example, we find it to be a suitable model for this task, and we also discover that its world knowledge contributes significantly, although intriguingly excessive knowledge can have a negative impact. Moreover, we adapt the model through two methods with progressive data masking levels, achieving more controlled regulation of its knowledge and maintaining its syntactic processing capabilities. This adaptation process showcases the versatility of BART's knowledge and the potential of its fine-tuning adaptability in provable language models.

The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable technique for identifying deepfakes. Deepfake creation methods inadvertently leave distinguishing patterns in the frequency spectra of fabricated images and videos. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces a novel detection method, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which combines features from spatial and frequency domains to derive a unified, discriminative representation for deepfake classification. The proposed network architecture, comprising two parallel branches processing spatial and frequency information, is designed to treat multiple domain inputs as interconnected learning signals. Through cross-stitch connections between the branches, our system automatically identifies an optimal blend of domain-specific and shared features, thereby enhancing performance and generalization. Evaluations conducted on the widely-used FaceForeniscs++ benchmark demonstrate improved classification results for various manipulation types and comparable performance to state-of-the-art approaches. Furthermore, the proposed method exhibits robust generalization capabilities.

Current studies examining the performance of randomly assembled low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes usually assume the independence of degree distributions from edge endpoints. In contrast, our research extends this understanding by investigating LDPC ensembles that incorporate degree-degree correlations. We propose novel methods for generating degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles, derive efficient techniques for calculating binary erasure channel (BEC) thresholds under general degree-degree correlations, and demonstrate how specific correlated LDPC configurations can exhibit significantly higher BEC thresholds compared to their uncorrelated counterparts. Furthermore, we establish a direct connection between degree-degree correlations and polygonal decomposition methods for assessing BEC thresholds of LDPC ensembles with diverse degree distributions.

A critical flaw exists in the current application of quantum key distribution (QKD) systems due to their vulnerability to quantum hacking. Our novel approach incorporates a hybrid measurement attack, achievable with only basic components such as linear optics, homodyne detection, and single photon detection, which poses a significant threat to the widely adopted vacuum+weak decoy state QKD system. Specifically, if the source phase is randomly altered to a limited degree, we discovered that the proposed attack can bypass the system's security, resulting in the entanglement-breaking channel without being detected by the users. Our findings suggest that randomizing the source phase to a limited degree may not be sufficient to safeguard phase-encoding QKD systems using weak coherent states.

To effectively manage the vast amounts of data being generated by a growing number of mobile and IoT devices, future mobile networks (MNs) must shift from traditional resource allocation methods. By integrating computation capabilities into Base Stations, we can optimize resource usage and efficiently manage resources near the edge of the network. Leveraging techniques such as time-series forecasting and control theory, we propose using neural networks and optimizing strategies within the Multi-access Edge Computing paradigm. Our approach involves online algorithms for virtualized resource scaling, reconfiguring computing and communication assets, and enabling dynamic BS switching to minimize energy consumption and ensure Quality of Service (QoS). Numerical results demonstrate that these strategies lead to significant reductions in edge computing and communication energy consumption, promoting energy self-sustainability in MNs through the use of green energy sources.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems.

Consider a number field $K$ of degree $n \geq 2$, embedded in the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$, and define its norm as the geometric mean of the squared absolute values of its $n$ embeddings. For any order $\mathcal{O}$ in $K$, the successive minima $\lambda_0 = 1 \leq \dots \leq \lambda_{n-1}$ with respect to this norm determine the inequality structure. Inspired by Lenstra's conjecture, we seek to characterize all inequalities of the form $1 \ll_{\mathcal{S}} \lambda_1^{f_1}\dots\lambda_{n-1}^{f_{n-1}}$, for an infinite set $\mathcal{S}$ of isomorphism classes of orders, for various sets $\mathcal{S}$, especially those based on field or subfield properties. For degrees $n$ with certain prime factorization properties (such as being prime powers or products of two primes), we establish a combinatorial classification of the integers defining relationships between minima and provide analogues of our results for ideals in number fields and curves, examining the interplay between minima and other geometric invariants.

We utilize 1-d fs/ps hybrid rotational coherent anti-Stokes Raman spectroscopy with dual probes to make comprehensive measurements of gas temperature, pressure, and oxygen-to-nitrogen ratios. By harnessing the power of time and frequency-domain measurements, a cutting-edge technique offers unprecedented accuracy (<1%) and precision (0.42%) for determining pressure. Initially demonstrated in a sealed environment over a pressure range (1-1.5 bar), the method effectively captures intricate pressure variations resulting from nitrous gas interacting with a solid surface in various states of flow. Notably, it can also detect very fine-scale pressure differences arising from the conversion of kinetic energy into pressure as well as distinct O2/N2 patterns formed by turbulent mixing processes.

The traditional theory of planetary formation through core accretion has limitations when explaining how small particles overcome early development obstacles in a protoplanetary disk. A more recent model proposes the viscous ring-instability to account for ring structures in protoplanetary disks. It suggests that particles may reduce the disk's conductivity, inhibiting the growth of instability. Using GPU-based simulations of interacting gas and dust, this study investigates this model's validity. As the disk evolves, ring structures become unstable, breaking into smaller whirlpools, and subsequently forming stable dust formations. These structures provide ideal environments for the growth of planetary building blocks through gravitational collapse and the streaming instability. Observational data on exoplanets supports this process and creates favorable conditions for planetary system formation.

Quantum Hall phases exhibit gapped behavior in the interior while supporting both chiral and neutral edge modes.  A specific setup involving a path that only includes neutral modes, essential for an electric current from the source to the drain, is examined here. When a source is biased in this circuit, it is observed that an electric current can be measured at the drain, provided that backscattering between opposing modes at the contact locations is present. The result shows that neutral modes hold relevant information and can be used for a nonlocal reconstruction of a dc charge current. The described protocol may be employed to detect any neutral mode that counter-propagates with respect to charge modes, and this detection approach is applicable not only to the edge modes of quantum Hall systems but also to systems possessing neutral modes that do not originate from quantum Hall effects. Finally, an experimental demonstration of this concept is proposed.

We introduce a rigid cluster model to achieve a representation of the quantum group U_q(g) for Lie algebras of type ADE. This involves establishing a natural isomorphism from the n-th exterior power of the standard module to a specific complex of the cluster module whose cohomology yields the required modules. Furthermore, in types A and D, we demonstrate that the natural maps within the complex are invertible, thereby confirming that the exterior power modules are cluster modules in these types.

In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD, based on the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD). Under specific conditions and a sufficiently large regularization parameter, we analytically prove that our algorithm achieves a rate of convergence of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/\sqrt{KT} + K/T\right)$. Furthermore, experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of DR-DSGD, yielding an improvement of up to $10\%$ in test accuracy over various data distributions on three public datasets. DR-DSGD exhibits greater communication efficiency, with reduced communication rounds required to reach peak accuracy compared to traditional DSGD, particularly in decentralized networks.

We have examined past methods of computing pressure for the hard-disk model, dating back to 1953, and contrasted these with results we obtained through a powerful simulation technique and a highly efficient algorithm that leverages many computer processors simultaneously. Like various simple scientific models, such as the Drosophila model, understanding the hard-disk model required significant effort. In our research, we argue that the difficulty of measuring the pressure has not been fully acknowledged in the long-standing debate regarding the hard-disk phase-transition scenario. Our paper provides the fundamental principles of the hard-disk model, defines the concept of pressure and presents new, unbiased methods of estimating it. Additionally, our paper describes different computational algorithms used for sampling and includes the outcomes of pressure calculations for clusters of up to 1000 hard disks. These results can aid future research by highlighting areas where further investigation is needed.

This paper examines jet modifications within a medium using JEWEL and PYTHIA 6.4, emphasizing uncertainties associated with perturbative scales, nuclear PDFs, and temperature variations of the medium at onset and transition points. Jet spectrum and nuclear modification factor data from the LHC are used for comparison with simulated results. Additionally, the influence of nuclear PDFs and the medium on jet structure is investigated through Lund plane analysis, and the interaction between nuclear PDF choice and medium parameters is explored.

Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme.

The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, and overall luminosity for all valid candidates and their stellar populations. We determined a light reduction range of 2.6 to 5.5 for the galaxy bulge, and identified candidate clusters with ages exceeding 8 billion years and masses over 3.5 billion solar masses. We mapped the observed locations of these clusters relative to their distance and light reduction, and found most to be situated above the galaxy's stellar disk plane. We also discovered clusters exhibiting significant variations in metal content and element abundance. These findings support the multichannel growth hypothesis, suggesting that cluster formation through multiple processes can reveal unique stellar components within each cluster that may hold the key to understanding their origins.

A set of precise theoretical and experimental benchmarks at hadron colliders are based on color-singlet differential spectra, known as exclusive differential spectra. Our study provides a comprehensive effective-theory framework, using soft-collinear effective theory to account for heavy-quark effects in differential distributions at various scale hierarchies, specifically considering the splitting of gluons into heavy-quark pairs alongside the primary contributions of heavy-quarks in hard-scattering processes. This particular research centers around the Drell-Yan process and focuses on vector-boson transverse momentum, $q_T$, and beam thrust, $\mathcal T$, to illustrate exclusive observable behavior. Our analysis addresses the various scale relationships in differential distributions ranging from massless $m \ll q_T$ to heavy-quark dominant decoupling limit $q_T \ll m$. To investigate quark-mass dependencies in an intermediate regime, precise numerical calculations utilizing beam functions from scale $Q$ to $m_F$ and matching function $m_F$ to mass scale $m$ have been conducted. Our study incorporates next-to-leading-order corrections for beam functions and next-to-leading-log resummation for $Q\, e^{-\gamma_E \ln\left(Q^2/m^2\right)}$, effectively capturing quark-mass effects across the broad scale regimes in $q_T$ distribution at the next-to-next-to-leading logarithmic to logarithmic accurate level, including both leading and subleading logarithmic contributions that have been

We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The conventional method of fitting these models involves translating the velocity gauge Hamiltonian into the equivalent form in the dipole gauge directly from first-principle calculations. Alternatively, we propose a straightforward procedure to construct a real-space Hubbard model in the velocity gauge, based on a real-space representation of a Hermitian Hamiltonian. We demonstrate that both approaches yield identical results. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of the gauge choice on a band-structure modification induced by a strong laser field. These findings indicate that theoretical models fitted from first-principle calculations must consistently adhere to a specific gauge framework. Our research also highlights the significance of employing the appropriate gauge when analyzing systems under the influence of external electromagnetic fields.

In this context, we explore certain classes of holographic tensor networks, which can efficiently simulate various systems using the principle of minimization, serve as quantum codes to prevent information loss, and accurately describe phenomena exhibiting power-law behaviors. A key finding reveals that networks comprising a single type of tensor and possessing erasure correction capabilities can't simultaneously possess certain desirable traits - those that facilitate the efficient calculation of physical properties through a local process and those necessary for an accurate representation of power-law behaviors in data. This contradiction motivates the creation of network guidelines that utilize diverse types of tensors, allowing these networks to successfully capture the characteristics of power-law behaviors while adhering to the principle of efficient calculation. A concrete example of such a network has also been developed - one that closely resembles the holographic HaPPY pentagon code under the assumption that specific system parameters can be set to a particular small range.

A theoretical analysis of retinal chromophore photoisomerization in rhodopsin utilized a model incorporating thermal baths and dual states. It was observed that quantum yields in a steady-state condition (occurring 10 ps after the reaction begins and onwards) differ notably from their short-lived counterparts, indicating an imperfect correlation between transient and sustained behaviors. Furthermore, the steady-state quantum yield was shown to be exquisitely sensitive to minor adjustments in system parameters, in stark contrast to the relative insensitivity of transient dynamics. Analysis of this sensitivity in relation to nonadiabatic vibronic level spacing suggests that quantum chaos might underlie this phenomenon, and potential avenues for experimental validation along with implications in complex light-sensitive systems are explored.

Deep-learning techniques such as Convolutional Neural Networks and Recurrent
Neural Networks have seen significant success in process-mining applications.
Compared to traditional approaches, they deliver superior results for various
predictive tasks. Our research expands on existing knowledge by testing five
different variants of deep learning models, including Graph Neural Networks and
Multi-layer Perceptron with dropout, for predicting the characteristics and
occurrence time of subsequent process events. Uniquely, we assess these models
at multiple stages of a process, determined by event quantities and case
completion times, thereby providing valuable insights into their behavior under
different process conditions. Our experiments surprisingly reveal that the basic
Multi-layer Perceptron frequently surpasses more advanced deep learning models
in both prediction tasks. Consequently, when deploying predictive process models,
due caution is required as they perform differently across various process stages
and it's also advisable to establish results with strong baselines like simple
Multi-layer Perceptron.

Turkey is prone to seismic activities with varying intensity earthquakes occurring frequently, emphasizing the necessity for swift and effective crisis information dissemination. Social media can provide valuable insights into public perception, beneficial for crisis communication and management. This research focuses on analyzing Twitter posts related to the 2020 Izmir earthquake, aiming to leverage these insights to infer real-time public opinions. By combining data mining and natural language processing techniques, we examine public sentiment and topic discussions following the earthquake. Our approach utilized LDA for topic modeling and BERT for sentiment analysis. Results show users shared supportive messages and engaged with relief efforts, expressing their desire to help the affected area. The implemented approach demonstrated success, and future work will explore advanced sentiment analysis methods and incorporate visual components for comprehensive topic modeling.

We investigate key properties of several types of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which are characterized by the decay of their smooth functions and their Fourier transforms. The nontriviality of these spaces, specifically ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_s$, is shown to depend on the values of $s$ and ${\sigma}$ being greater than 1. The text further presents growth estimates for functions within one-parameter spaces, and it also establishes relationships between short-time Fourier transforms and these spaces. Moreover, conditions are established to ensure that Toeplitz operators are continuous when applied to functions within one-parameter spaces.

Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry, which in turn provides a critical benchmark for identifying potential biosignatures on exoplanets. As we've been able to curate large catalogs of nearby, Sun-like stars suitable for EXScMoS, our goal is to assess how many of these stars exhibit white-light flactivity, and if they are capable of producing detectable white-light flactivity that could potentially be seen from an exoplanet. Using the HATPETS, KEPLER, and K2 data sets, we detected 847 individual white-light flares across 146 SUn-like stars, and we found that 60% of these stars are likely to exhibit observable white-light flactivity, with 10 of them having a good chance of producing biosignature-relevant white-light flactivity with current or future space-based telescopes. Notably, we found that all Kepler and K2 targets that showed a high signal-to-noise ratio during the full-Kepler/K2 mission, including 7 similar to the Sun, are found to exhibit bio-relevant white-light flactivity, with potential biosignature relevant effects during fullKepler/K2 observations.

This investigation into the PT-symmetric waveguide network's behavior uses mathematical models to derive exact equations describing wave propagation in a finite number of connected units. Analyzing this through generalized parametric space, researchers discovered that when PT symmetry breaks, propagating modes appear consistently, unaffected by the unit cell's transmission phase or number. However, at PT-symmetric equilibrium, mode formation relies on the unit cell's transmission phase. Notably, reflectionless and perfectly transmissible states can be achieved by selecting specific PT phases and numbers of connected units. Two methods were identified to induce CPAL - operating an odd-numbered series of units at a specific point or using a particular broken phase in conjunction with an allotropic transmission phase in multiple units. This research provides theoretical groundwork for PT-symmetric photonics, enabling a deeper understanding and control of extraordinary light phenomena.

We study the behavior and evolution of Boolean networks with sparse connections that interact with themselves using Glauber dynamics, where the dynamics occurs simultaneously for all elements in the network. Equilibrium is evaluated by modifying and applying a method for systems that update in parallel. Similarly, dynamic behavior can be assessed using an advanced version of the method for systems that update at different times. Nonetheless, applying this technique to networks that interact with themselves is challenging because it causes the network to rely heavily on past events, making it difficult to model the network's behavior over extended periods of time. However, it has been proven possible to transform the network into an equivalent bipartite network with double the variables, allowing for analysis of systems that interact with themselves using traditional methods. This breakthrough enables a deeper examination of how systems behave during transitional and extended periods of time. Lastly, we investigate networks that interact with multiple components and are utilized in gene regulation systems by transforming these systems into equivalent bipartite networks, which consist of two sets of genes that interact with each other using ordinary dynamics. It is shown that these systems exhibit distinct behaviors during transitional periods compared to those that interact with multiple components, and that their equilibrium can be effectively modeled using a simplified network through our proposed method.

We derive concise mathematical expressions for calculating matrix elements of single-particle and particle-particle operators that can be applied to a wide range of Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov wave functions, encompassing configurations involving multiple quasiparticle excitations. Furthermore, our test simulations demonstrate the significant potential of these formulas to streamline the restoration of symmetry within large and complex nuclear systems.

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation, but they're prone to deception from legitimate-appearing 3D transformations. To improve robustness, we identified and addressed a key weakness in current evaluation methods for transformational adversarial examples (TAEs). Instead of randomly generating 3D transformations, we categorized them into three groups: simple, moderate, and complex. Our study revealed that existing benchmarks only covered the complex category. We introduced an ensemble evaluation method to fairly compare model performances across all categories and found current measures of adversarial success rely solely on the most complex category. As for complexity, we view moderate and moderate and simple combinations as moderate combinations. As for moderate and simple combinations as moderate. We proposed using this new evaluation framework on the way. We also suggested a new evaluation method using this new framework. We introduced our evaluation method using this new framework. We also developed RC-TPN, a more robust model that outperformed existing models across all categories in our evaluation framework.

We're investigating medium access techniques in Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks with all radar units utilizing identical settings, such as sweep duration and frequency characteristics. We're developing and evaluating the performance of contention-free network configurations, where each radar unit operates on a distinct frequency channel, and comparable slotted ALOHA-based randomized networks, in which the FMCW protocol incorporates a clear channel assessment (listening before transmitting) to reduce the likelihood of collisions, and in which we analyze and evaluate the impact of the clear channel assessment on the success rate of data transmissions, and our findings are backed up by simulation results, and our code is openly available online, at the address: https://github.com/zhengyan04/omnetpp_fmcw.

Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building upon successful applications of tensor decomposition in static graph
completions, we introduce Time-LowFER - an extension of the low-rank factorization
model that is both efficient in parameters and attentive to time constraints.
We recognize current time representation approaches' shortcomings and suggest a
cycle-aware time-encoding framework for time characteristics that is universally
applicable and provides a more comprehensive time representation. Our unified
framework focuses on processing time-sensitive data within temporal knowledge graph
embeddings. Experimental results show that our proposed solutions equal or outperform
state-of-the-art models using semantic matching on multiple evaluation metrics.

Within the RPA framework, the Jost function method has been employed to examine
the structure of $^{16}$O electric dipole excitement. Previous research has
indicated that the dominant component of this excitement, a significant resonance
feature around 20-30 MeV, lacks a clear analogy to traditional compound nucleus
resonances due to its high-energy range. Despite numerous studies on $^{16}$O
excitement, there's still insufficient information to precisely determine its
underlying mechanism. To address this limitation, we have expanded our previous
research by utilizing a broader range of test functions, encompassing both
step-function and fermionic types. Furthermore, the impact of continuum
discreteness has been thoroughly investigated within this enhanced framework.
The results show that the resonance's existence is firmly established, with its
position largely unaffected by the test function choice, and its frequency is
consistent with previous findings, remaining around 21.5 within 19.5-23.5 MeV.
However, the impact of discrete density states on the resonance frequency and its
amplitude has been found to vary significantly, with test functions yielding
different outcomes. The RPA approach within the continuum random phase approximation
has demonstrated the capability to represent the excited states of nuclear systems
more comprehensively than traditional methods have achieved so far.

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest.

Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the adversarial nature of training makes it hard to converge. This issue is exacerbated when working with data from open-domain social media. In this study, we investigate the application of GANs to text generation and explore whether a simpler, non-adversarial approach can be effective. We propose an algorithm that adapts the BERT-based pre-trained language model for text generation, building on the use of BERT for decoding. Our algorithm delivers comparable results to the GAN-based method while being significantly more efficient to train and compute.

The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has its roots in the distant past, but the challenge remains of being able to observe this theory in action. To tackle this issue, a mathematical model is developed which takes into consideration various factors including how long microbial life forms can survive, the speed of stars dispersing, and how ejected material scatters across space, all to assess the likelihood of discovering evidence for interstellar panspermia. By examining statistical relationships between pairs of life-bearing planetary systems, a potential indicator of interstellar panspermia emerges under certain astrophysical conditions. Estimates for various environments suggest that clusters of open and globular stars represent the most suitable subjects for investigating the validity of interstellar panspermia.

Using the Effective Field Theory of Large Scale Structure, we make predictions for HI intensity mapping power spectrum multipoles based on perturbation theory. These predictions will allow us to constrain cosmological parameters using mildly non-linear scales from data that will be obtained from interferometric HI intensity mapping experiments. Assuming that the experiments will be like CHORD and PUMA, we run a series of analyses on mock data, and compare these to the accuracy that can be achieved using N-body simulations combined with radiative transfer to generate redshift space maps. Both CHORD and PUMA are assumed to be using 21 cm field data at 1<z<3, with a radial redshift range of 100 h^{-1} Mpc. We derive effective observables within the EFT framework that are least affected by systematics associated with the volume and configuration of the survey, which we call the configuration-weighted power and void-enhanced multipoles. Initially, we verify that these mock quantities follow the expected form from the EFT, before using them to constrain the values of four cosmological parameters that affect the matter power spectrum, by comparing to a four-parameter fiducial model. These estimators are able to recover the correct four combinations of parameters from the mock data, with a total error of $\sigma^2_{tot}=\sigma^2_{cosm}+\sigma^2_{bias}\approx (0.6-1.0)^2$, with the higher values

The proposed concept of induced spontaneous symmetry breaking is explored through a theoretical scenario. This scenario posits that spontaneous symmetry breaking occurs at the highest energy level, causing a cascade of symmetry violations at lower energy levels resulting from subtle mixings between them. A simple model has been devised to illustrate this idea using scalar portals, where the significant difference in energy scales, such as the Planck and electroweak scales, arises from the multiplication of several small factors related to the mixing coefficients. The formation of dark matter fields is also examined in this framework, where it is possible for these fields to emerge from matter fields located on one or more intermediate energy levels between the highest and lowest.

Animal population studies often prioritize assessing the effects of human impacts, yet they require extensive data collection in the field. A lesser studied aspect of wildlife interaction with their environment is their habitat selection, which can be inferred from GPS tracking information. From movement data, we can derive contextual environmental information, although this method has its limitations. Nevertheless, many animals' populations remain stable, making inference possible from available tracking data. Numerous methods exist for analyzing such data, including those based on case-control and matching approaches. This study focuses on resource selection functions (RSFs), which model the relationship between animals and their environmental surroundings. These models can be enhanced by incorporating spatial selection components, accounting for the mobility of animals and their tendency to return to familiar areas. A generalized linear mixed model was developed to handle these spatial components, enabling more accurate modeling of animals' selection behaviors. This method was tested on brown bear data, but is applicable to any species with location and context information.

In designing minimum power networks, we are given an undirected graph $G = (V, E)$ along with associated edge costs. The objective is to select an edge subset $F \subseteq E$ satisfying a specific minimum power criterion. Specifically, for the Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problem, F must contain exactly k disjoint st-paths. Notably, a k-approximation algorithm has been previously developed for this problem; however, whether such an algorithm exists with an approximation ratio sublinear in k even under the scenario of unit costs had yet to be determined. We present a new $4\sqrt{2k}$-approximation algorithm applicable to general cost settings.

This study proposes a technique for the autonomous planning of swarms of unmanned aerial vehicles within a predefined environment. When the swarm detects changes, such as the movement of a target, within a designated area, the command center recalculates and adjusts the swarm's flight path. Key algorithms employed in this research are A* pathfinding and Generalized Labeled Multi-Bernoulli for target tracking.

The concept of localization in physics is significant in understanding dynamic processes on complex networks, particularly near critical transitions. This study tackles this issue by measuring nodal activity to quantify localization in networks undergoing dynamic changes. The proposed method is widely applicable and can be employed with theoretical models, simulated data, and real-world observations. The researchers analyze spreading processes on various networks, demonstrating that nodal activity can display intricate patterns depending on the network's architecture. The findings indicate that localized and widespread patterns are not mutually exclusive features in a spreading process. Additionally, the prevalence of an epidemic near a critical transition is influenced by the delocalized component of the network. Furthermore, different critical exponents can coexist with similar localization patterns. The study also reveals a more intricate behavior in quenched networks, influenced by the type of activation and degree exponent. The work sets the stage for future investigations of localized activity in network processes.

Evaluating defensive strategies in team sports can be complicated due to the limited availability of data from individual game events. Previous researchers developed methods for assessing football teams' defensive prowess by predicting the likelihood of gaining possession of the ball and being attacked, based on the location of all players involved. These earlier approaches, however, underestimated the importance of such events, as they occur less frequently, leading to more significant implications, and neglected the circumstances resulting from scoring goals, which also rely heavily on a team's defensive performance. Our novel approach mitigates these limitations by analyzing the all-play-all player configurations at the moment of every event, allowing for more accurate and comparable predictions, and ultimately revealing distinct defensive performance metrics with clear rankings of top and bottom teams, as well as Liguette's unexpected performance at the bottom.

Extracting information from images of forms is a complex task due to varying layout designs. This complexity increases with old forms that have deteriorated and are contaminated with noise. One crucial step in the extraction process involves linking input text to predefined label fields. Our research offers an innovative, layout-agnostic method to identify pre-printed text, handwriting, and their relationships. Our technique excels in handling imperfect form images, unlike previous approaches designed for well-organized images. To test its effectiveness, we created a database of deteriorated forms from the late 1800s and early 1900s. Our model uses a neural network to identify both types of text, after which we classify their relationships through the analysis of the detected text features. Our research indicates that our relationship-determination technique performs better than rule-based methods and confirms that visual features play a key role in achieving high accuracy in these situations.

Highly flexible recurrent state-space models can capture complex patterns in time series data, but typically assume a static and unchanging dynamic, a rare occurrence in real-world situations. To overcome this limitation, many systems exhibit patterns that are similar yet distinct, and can be described through a single underlying variable. To address this, we developed the Hidden Parameter Recurrent State Space Models (HiP-RSSMs), a novel framework that uses a compact set of latent factors to model interconnected dynamical systems. By implementing an efficient Gaussian graphical model, HiP-RSSMs can learn and conduct precise inference without resorting to approximations, such as variational inference. In our experiments, HiP-RSSMs consistently surpassed traditional state-space models and multi-task competitors on multiple demanding robotic tasks, in both real-world applications and simulations.

Independent unitarily invariant $N\times N$ random matrices exhibit expected asymptotic freeness to $O(N^{-2})$. Infinitesimal freeness in expectation is already known to result from this property. We've established an additional consequence: almost sure asymptotic freeness of type $B$ for unitarily invariant random matrices. This consequence leads to several secondary findings: the asymptotic cyclic monotonicity, and the derivation of asymptotic conditional freeness. Specifically, we demonstrate the empirical spectral distribution of randomly rotated matrices converges towards a conditionally free convolution. We've also identified new relationships between infinitesimal freeness, type $B$ freeness, conditional freeness, cyclic monotonicity, and monotone independence. Moreover, we show that the BBP phase transition in an additive rank-one perturbation of a GUE matrix is a consequence of asymptotic conditional freeness. This line of reasoning applies as well to an analysis of outlier eigenvalues in various unitarily invariant ensembles.

We take a degree-2 cover of a genus-1 curve D over a non-hyperelliptic genus-3 curve C, in a field of characteristic not 2. We construct a genus-2 curve X, such that its Jacobian is connected to a product of the Jacobian of D and X's Jacobian, the Jacobian of C being an isogeny.

Determining the extent of polarization within social systems is vital to studying its effects on political structures. While numerous methods are employed to analyze polarization in social networks through structural evaluation, our analysis revealed that eight commonly used methods yield elevated polarization scores even in artificially constructed networks that closely mirror real-world networks in density and distribution. Furthermore, some of these methods proved sensitive to specific characteristics of polarized groups, such as degree distribution and size. We proposed introducing a standard normalization to mitigate these issues, alongside a comprehensive set of criteria for effective structural measurement of polarization. By normalizing the scores, many methods demonstrated significantly improved performance, with some achieving substantial increases in accuracy, notably nearly 50% better than non-normalized results. Notably, we discovered that the K-clique method, when normalized, outperformed other commonly used measurement methods.

The analysis of multilayer networks has been utilized to model various dynamic systems, offering a more accurate representation than single-layer networks, albeit at the cost of increased analytical complexity. To overcome this challenge, we present a method for examining the dynamics of Kuramoto oscillators within multilayer networks by applying a joint matrix representation. This technique provides a compact representation of the multilayer system that maintains equivalent dynamics. As a result, we can determine solutions for the reduced system and then extend them to the multilayer network. Furthermore, we can investigate the stability of these solutions by analyzing the reduced system and obtaining insights into the multilayer system's Jacobian. Our method is adaptable to different interlayer node connections. Ultimately, our research enables the exploration of multilayer networks through simplified representations, facilitating a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics underlying these systems.

Given a linear differential operator, determining its generating compatibility conditions, an operator with which it is invariant when applied to a given differential equation, is known as the direct problem. This process yields successive first-order operators for an n-dimensional manifold. The converse, an inverse problem, is to find the original differential operator when one of these compatibility operators is known. The compatibility operator can be parameterized by the original differential operator only if it defines a torsion-free differential module. The parametrization is minimal when this differential module has a vanishing differential rank. Notably, attempts to parameterize the Cauchy stress operator have been a subject of study for renowned scientists such as G.B. Airy, J.C. Maxwell, and A. Einstein. This work identifies a widespread misconception among them, mistakenly using the Einstein operator and confusing it with the Cauchy operator and the $div$ operator induced from the Bianchi operator. As an interesting aside, determining whether Einstein was aware of previous work is a historical puzzle.

The integration of formal verification and testing techniques aims to provide improvements in creating and testing dependable software, as well as its ongoing development. Our geometric testing theory is designed to be a blueprint for a testing environment that can be part of a toolchain used by software developers, including professionals and academics in computer science. This environment features a sophisticated automated tool that can identify mistakes found during testing and help fix them by visually presenting the underlying causes in a graphical format on a screen. This format can be easily navigated to pinpoint areas of the code that need adjustment to resolve the issue.

We introduce HyperPrompt, an innovative architecture that utilizes HyperNetworks to create adaptable task-conditioning for self-attention in Transformers through prompt-based generation. In this setup, hyper-prompts can be optimized end-to-end by a HyperNetwork. By employing hyper-prompts as global task memories, HyperPrompt enables networks to learn task-specific features while facilitating flexible sharing of general features. This approach allows for the development of highly efficient inference systems with multiple task handling capabilities in a single network, reducing both memory and computation requirements. We demonstrate HyperPrompt's effectiveness by adapting the HyperPrompt-based HyperNetwork on Top-2 Hyper-gates, achieving outstanding results with exceptionally low in-situ memory requirements of just O(O(d)). Furthermore, we introduce an efficient in-situ in-sampling method for hyper-prompts, enabling flexible sharing of task-specific features. Experiments on the LAMA image captioning benchmark with pre-trained TGLA demonstrate HyperPrompt's superior performance, achieving 20.04 BLEU-4 with only a 1.7x increase in in-situ memory requirements (O(O(d))) while handling up to 32 tasks. By utilizing the same network for all tasks, HyperPrompt achieves an in-situ memory requirement of just O(4*d*) with the same or better performance, while also significantly reducing computation requirements by a factor of K times that of K separate attention networks.

Let $\Phi$ be a root system belonging to type $A_l$ or $D_l$. Let $K$ be a field whose characteristic is not $2$. Let $\delta$ be the maximal root in the root system $\Phi$ and define the set $\Phi_0$ as consisting of the roots $\alpha$ in $\Phi$ for which $\alpha$ is orthogonal to $\delta$. The group $G_{\text{sc}}(\Phi_0, K)$ is then described as acting on the set containing elements of the form $e_\alpha$, with the condition that the angle between $\alpha$ and $\delta$ is $\frac{\pi}{3}$.

In the ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity QED, we show that symmetry protects a type of photon bundle emission. The parity symmetry of the Rabi model allows for the creation of super-Rabi oscillations, resulting in the periodic production of even photons in the cavity. This phenomenon occurs through a laser-driven qubit flip and transitions influenced by Rabi interaction, preserving parity. By introducing dissipation, the system only emits photons in 2$n$ correlations, and this emission's purity is improved by the parity symmetry, mainly due to reduced odd-correlated photon emissions. The parity symmetry of the system can be controlled and adjusted with a magnetic field, and we demonstrate that the protection of this symmetry enhances the 2$n$-correlated photon emission. This research may enable the study of super-Rabi dynamics and develop a solid-state even-photon source.

We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. Furthermore, the algorithm executes within O(log^3(n)) rounds, necessitates nodes to transmit small data packets in each round, and entails a minimal computation expense per round for each node.

Accurate traffic management heavily relies on reliable traffic state estimation.
This study introduces a novel nonparametric approach to estimate short-term
queue lengths without assuming random arrivals or estimating specific parameters.
The method, which uses simple mathematical expressions based solely on traffic
signal timing, estimates conditional queue lengths for an approach lane at an
intersection. Specifically, a Negative Hypergeometric distribution models these
estimates, which are compared to existing parametric methods using real-world data
from probe vehicles. The findings suggest that the proposed nonparametric
methodology matches the accuracy of traditional methods used in the field study.

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data.
