Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds.

The search for $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decays utilizing $pp$ collision data collected by LHCb, at centre-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV and an accumulated luminosity of 3 $fb^{-1}$, yields 4 standard deviation excess beyond predicted background counts with no noticeable features found in dimuon invariant mass spectra.

Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a joint experimental and theoretical approach. Our experimental findings, combined with a DFT analysis, reveal a substantial anomalous Nernst coefficient of approximately 5.8 $\mu$V/V/K at 300 K, with potential applications in thermally driven spin-transfer-tunneling magnetic devices.

Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted ranking systems, delivering outstanding results. To balance high performance with computational efficiency, knowledge distillation is now extensively employed. In this research, we address two critical challenges in knowledge distillation for ranking models: 1) leveraging multiple teachers; and 2) utilizing label data within the distillation process. We introduce the Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE) framework to concurrently address both concerns. By iteratively combining multi-teacher logits guided by label information, PILE has shown superior performance in offline and online experiments. Furthermore, our method has been successfully integrated into a real-world commercial search platform.

This lecture will provide an elementary overview of both transverse and longitudinal beam dynamics, in addition to key beam loss phenomena in circular accelerators, catering to attendees with minimal to no prior understanding of this topic.

Understanding and identifying functional materials rely heavily on imaging, scattering, and spectroscopy. Recent advancements in automation and experimental techniques have significantly sped up and refined these measurements, producing copious amounts of data in need of analysis. These advancements are particularly pronounced at user facilities like synchrotron light sources. To process and interpret large datasets quickly, machine learning methods are continually being developed for real-time use in conjunction with measurements. Despite these developments, users without machine learning expertise often face significant barriers to integrating this technology into their experiments. To overcome these obstacles, this work presents several examples of machine learning models designed for real-time analysis across multiple beamlines at the National Synchrotron Light Source II (NSLS-II), with a focus on incorporating them into existing workflows to enable easy integration into experiments. By leveraging this generalizable framework, users can easily combine pre-trained models with their measurements, tailored to their specific needs and hardware setup.

We have derived improved differentiability properties for solutions to a non-autonomous obstacle problem, formulated as
  \begin{equation*}
  \min \left\{\int_{\Omega}f\left(x, Dv(x)\right)dx\,:\, v\in
  \mathcal{K}_\psi(\Omega)\right\}.
  \end{equation*} Given the growth restrictions imposed on the function $f$, with respect to the gradient variable, we find that where the obstacle condition is not active, the map $x\mapsto f(x,\xi)$ must meet a specific growth requirement, which is autonomic in nature, thereby allowing for obstacles with varying degrees of regularity, including Dini continuous obstacles.

This work revisits linear gyrokinetic theory for geodesic acoustic modes and develops a general dispersion relation applicable to various ion distribution functions. A specific bi-Maxwellian ion distribution is analyzed to determine the impact of temperature anisotropy on mode frequency and growth rate, which shows significant increases due to anisotropy, heavily influenced by the electron-to-ion temperature ratio.

A promising technique known as quantum annealing has been proposed for efficiently solving combinatorial optimization problems embedded in the Ising model's ground state. This approach involves two distinct types of Hamiltonians: a driver Hamiltonian whose ground state is easily prepared and a problem Hamiltonian whose ground state corresponds to the optimal solution. By gradually transforming the driver Hamiltonian into the problem Hamiltonian, one can attempt to reach this optimal solution. In this study, we introduce a novel class of non-stoquastic Hamiltonians featuring anti-ferromagnetic interactions and demonstrate that certain problems, including those with localized solutions and others whose solutions spread uniformly across the configuration space, can be efficiently reached via quantum annealing. Notably, we find that the presence of anti-ferromagnetic interactions results in a reduced stagnation time, thus reducing the likelihood of getting trapped in metastable states during quantum annealing.

This essay explores the development of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory from 1921 to 1957, during the tenure of director Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, who succeeded the lab's founder, Jacobus Cornelius Kapteyn. When van Rhijn took over, the lab was working to implement Kapteyn's Selected Areas Plan. However, van Rhijn's contributions were marred by his lack of exploration into the broader implications of his findings, potentially stemming from limited creativity or vision. Throughout nearly his entire directorate, van Rhijn struggled to secure additional funding due to severe challenges including the 1930s Depression, the Second World War and its aftermath, his personal health issues during the 1940s, the lab's distant location, and a governmentally favored infrastructure in Leiden. Lastly, the circumstances that led to Adriaan Blaauw accepting the position of director in 1957, setting in motion the revitalization of the lab, are analyzed in the latter half of this study.

We provide a detailed explanation for a part of Serre's conjecture related to GL_2 through Kummer theory, thereby bypassing the reliance on p-adic Hodge theory. This involves utilizing descriptions of crystalline extension reductions, Kummer theory, Abrashkin's findings, local class field theory, Dembele-Diamond-Roberts' earlier work, Brueckner-Shaferevich-Vostokov's reciprocity laws and their implications to describe and calculate certain G_K-Artin-Scheier cocycles.

We develop a comprehensive theory for optimal solutions in an isoperimetric problem outside a confined object within the setting of sets with limited perimeter in the n-dimensional space. This theoretical framework includes a detailed examination of specific structures that frequently appear as minimal shapes, such as those with an infinite extent, closed shapes that within any given area have a positive minimum size, and shapes within any given area that have a consistently limited size. A key component of this theory involves the identification of 'isoperimetric residues', which can be broken down into distinct parts representing open and compact shapes, respectively. This breakdown is not only unique but also essential in determining the structure of these shapes. A similar breakdown of this problem's density function contributes to these results. Some of our findings include the determination of when an open shape or a specific local shape can exist, as well as the establishment of a relationship between these shapes and a specific density function, thus providing an answer to a question posed by Colding and Minicozzi. These findings for shapes with limited perimeter also apply to shapes formed by smooth boundaries in the m n n R n d , , , -dimensional space.

This paper introduces an innovative approach called local critic training, a model-parallel learning method utilizing specialized networks to refine neural network updates. By segmenting the main network into separate layer groups and applying error gradients from corresponding critic modules, the learning process is efficiently decoupled, allowing different parts of the network to be trained independently. We demonstrate that this method not only converges to an optimal solution but also offers several key advantages. Firstly, local critic networks significantly reduce communication during training, resulting in decreased latency and optimal scalability, as demonstrated by experiments on large-scale datasets like ImageNet. Furthermore, local critic training enables different parts of the neural network to adapt differentially, decoupling the generalization capabilities of various network components. This method also simplifies the deployment process by allowing different server parts to be placed in geographically distributed locations. Our approach represents a significant step forward in parallel learning, with potential applications in distributed systems and neural network specialization.

Advanced composite materials that incorporate nanofillers into polymer matrices have a vast potential for self-diagnostic capabilities through their inherent electrical conductivity. While the exact mechanism behind the change in composite conductivity due to damage remains unclear, this research utilizes molecular dynamics simulations to examine the internal structure of unidirectional carbon fiber composites with added carbon nanotubes. It's demonstrated that damage induces cracks within the fiber matrix, disrupting the conductive network. By applying the network percolation theory, the simulation results can be used to quantify the composite conductivity based on its microstructural characteristics, and this relationship shows significant potential for damage estimation. Furthermore, machine learning models can accurately predict the conductivity based on its mathematical derivation from the microstructure, and these predictions can in turn be used to estimate the extent of damage in the composite.

We're exploring the possibility that there's a parallel between brain neurons and societal individuals, inquiring whether collective intelligence requires individual intellect and what specific forms of individual knowledge contribute to greater collective insight. By integrating principles from connectionism, agent-based modeling, group psychology, economics, and physics, we reframe these concepts through the lens of changing system dynamics. Ultimately, we apply this understanding to explain the coexistence of prey and predator species in the Lotka-Volterra model and the catastrophic consequences of particular individual intellect applications.

We have designed a novel control method using learning algorithms for complex systems whose behavior is unknown. This algorithm excels in environments where there is only limited, high-noise data from ongoing experiments. It achieves exceptional results by making the most of various types of secondary information, including observations from related dynamical models and analogous learning algorithms. The method essentially employs a probabilistic framework to integrate this additional information with real-world data, enabling the derivation of an optimal action plan. The proposed algorithm is illustrated through numerous numerical examples, encompassing purely data-driven learning, as well as the management of unknown and complex systems using renowned models such as the Lorenz attractor.

This work proposes a tensor framework for Euclidean spaces centered on geometric vector techniques and illustrates the method's efficacy through a variety of vector integrand identities proved using this framework.

A theoretical model involving an intricate scalar sector, which involves an intricate connection between the observed 54 GeV γγ resonance and a lengthy trajectory between production and decay due to slow-moving leptons created in interactions with standard model gauge forces, can potentially offer a substantial indication of new physics if this novel sector has an influential connection with dark matter.

This investigation explores the impact of remote learning during the COVID pandemic on the ability of university students to keep up with the pace of instruction in a physics course. Focusing on the varying effects of remote learning on diverse demographic groups, data was collected from online learning modules in the Fall 2020 and Spring 2020 semesters. Comparing students' module submission rates before and during the pandemic, as well as their performance on in-class assessments, revealed significant disparities. First-generation students experiencing difficulty keeping up with instruction showed increased difficulty submitting modules, whereas students from underrepresented racial and ethnic backgrounds demonstrated no such difference. Additionally, students who struggled to stay current with instruction performed worse on written evaluations and in-class tests. These findings underscore the adverse effects of remote learning on students' ability to stay on pace with instruction and the importance of staying current with the material for long-term success.

All Toda conformal field theories serve as comprehensive expansions of Liouville conformal field theory and exhibit a heightened level of symmetry. Within Toda conformal field theories, this higher-spin symmetry is made apparent by an underlying algebraic framework, allowing for precise derivation of their basic properties. Notably, the bootstrap approach is applicable to these theories due to this inherent structure, though specifically for real-form Toda theories, this yields constraints on possible spinning four-point correlations rather than reflecting the theories' genuine spinorial characteristics. This generalised form of the bootstrap is examined across various Toda theories, revealing relationships between seemingly distinct real-form theories that were not previously recognized. As an illustration, it is shown how the properties of $PSU(n|n)$ super-Liouville theory can be reduced to those of Liouville-Cosinh conformal field theory. Furthermore, the analysis implies that the effective central charge is also amenable to such generalisation.
We demonstrate that Coxeter groups possess biautomatic properties, resulting from which we derive that uniform lattices within isometry groups of buildings also exhibit biautomatic structures.

Investigating the thermodynamics and cosmic censorship conjecture in Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes through scalar field scattering yields results that support the first law of thermodynamics for non-extremal black holes, confirming that the singularity in such black holes is hidden by an event horizon. The validity of this theory for near-extremal and extremal black holes is confirmed by analyzing their minimum function values after the scattering process. The findings show that neither near-extremal nor extremal black holes can become overcharged due to such processes. The outcome of scattering when a certain relationship between the electric potential and scalar field is met is that the extremal black hole retains its extreme properties. In contrast, when this relationship is not met, the scattering causes the extremal black hole to transform into a near-extremal black hole with a different mass and charge configuration.

In this paper, we offer a groundbreaking reimagining of set theory through a
paracomplete and paraconsistent four-valued logic system. Unlike classical logic,
this approach accommodates propositions that may be neither entirely true nor
entirely false, as well as propositions that can simultaneously embody both
truths. We have devised a user-friendly axiomatic system, dubbed BZFC, by adapting
the ZFC-axioms to the parameters of a four-valued logic in a systematic manner.
Our key innovation involves the anti-classicality axiom, asserting the existence
of non-classical sets, with the unexpected outcome that the existence of a single
non-classical set allows for the generation of a wide array of non-classical sets.
Furthermore, our analysis encompasses the relationship between our proposed system
BZFC and classical ZFC, demonstrating that the two logics exhibit bidirectional
interpretability. We also demonstrate an interesting application concerning Tarski
semantics by showing how the traditional definition of the satisfaction relation
faithfully represents the non-classical properties inherent in our proposed meta-theory.

Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. To address this challenge, researchers utilized high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill. The analysis revealed a high level of accuracy (99.8%) in predicting walking state and step rate information from the recorded signals over extended periods (>10 minutes). Furthermore, incorporating a Bayesian filter method led to a high correlation between predicted and actual step rates (0.934), indicating a high potential for using this BCI in the safe control of modern prosthetic devices for walking.

This paper proposes a new computational method to estimate uncertainty and relevance metrics, like Shannon entropy and mutual information, for complex probability distributions that can't be directly calculated. By leveraging Nested Sampling, this approach enables evaluation of such quantities even when only sampling data is available. Three case studies are provided to illustrate its effectiveness: one with a straightforward Gaussian distribution; another with a real-world experiment involving observation scheduling for signal period estimation; and a scenario with predicting future outcomes from past data under heavy-tailed conditions.

If a right-angled Artin group acting minimally on a tree that is not a line has a non-trivial action, we prove that its graph $\Gamma$ contains a connected component whose subgroup acts transitively on an edge of the tree.

This paper examines a common approach to modeling complex, dynamic environments: representing the connectivity structure as a static graph. While this method has seen significant progress, mainly through advances in representation learning, we believe it's crucial to investigate more fundamental questions about the underlying graph. Our interest lies in understanding whether a fixed graph can effectively model the connectivity structure, or if the graph itself changes over time. To explore this, we develop a simple framework for learning a time-varying graph from supervised data. Our experiments demonstrate that using this framework to learn from noise-affected data results in more accurate models, compared to traditional methods, and that incorporating a more flexible graph into the system allows for better system performance. Moreover, our findings suggest that the system's performance can be significantly improved if the underlying assumption of a fixed graph is no longer constrained. Although this research uses reinforcement learning as an example, the concepts developed here are applicable to a wide range of models that rely on graphical representations.

Phylogenetic networks serve as a detailed representation of the evolutionary histories of various species, enabling them to incorporate reticulate evolutionary mechanisms such as lateral gene transfer and gene recombination. In contrast to phylogenetic trees, these networks provide a more comprehensive view of the evolutionary process. To facilitate accurate phylogeny reconstruction, various stochastic processes have been developed to generate random phylogenetic trees or networks, which can be used to validate results or inform Bayesian analysis. Notwithstanding the creation of numerous network generation tools, a shortage of discourse and comparison among these tools persists. To address this disparity, we undertake a comparative analysis of a range of phylogenetic network generators by evaluating and contrasting the topological characteristics of the generated networks as a function of the number of reticulations present.

Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, social interaction, survival, and reproduction. The ability to perform these actions is crucial to the survival of the species. Understanding the reasons behind animal movement can provide valuable insights into their overall behavior. Machine learning models that aim to predict and generate animal movement in their natural habitats need to incorporate the actions driven by these survival-based motives. In this study, we introduce a straightforward and effective method to model animal movement in an ecosystem, where the primary focus is on capturing the underlying motivation for locomotion. We frame this problem as a sub-goal conditioned movement generation task. Each sub-goal represents a distinct action such as hunting, engaging in social interaction, or repelling rivals. Using a variation of the conditional diffusion model, we train our framework to produce target behaviors and combine them with non-target actions to achieve the desired goal. We validate our approach using a dataset of six species from the San Diego Zoo, including ants, frogs, geckos, lions, penguins, and rats. The results from our study show a significant improvement in the frequency of target behavior occurrences when comparing our model to baseline methods. Moreover, our results demonstrate that our sub-goal conditioned generation can effectively generate specific actions and also leads to enhanced longevity when simulating these animals' movement.

The advent of big data processing has created significant computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion, prompting the development of fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods. Leveraging GPU acceleration, researchers have explored alternatives to classic direct inversion, leading to the creation of a new iterative method that combines elements of several existing methods, including LU decomposition, the normal equations, and the Cholesky decomposition. This novel algorithm excels in producing more accurate results with fewer GPU resources, offering an advantage of up to 10 times better precision at 10 times less error for certain methods, and best overall performance on multiple benchmark tests.

In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates incident wave patterns with internal distributions within a volume, and previously this correlation was leveraged to increase energy delivered to a target. This study determines a general set of constraints and formulas governing the eigenvalues and modes within any given scattering setup - including complex geometries, and broad categories such as slabs and narrow channels. Our mathematical framework reveals limitations and correlations for intensity within system boundaries, and derived properties apply universally to different types and strengths of wave, and multiple wave types.

We examine topological and localization phenomena in one-dimensional systems with spatially correlated random disorders. This study explores the effect of binary disorders on a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Our findings show that binary disorders can induce a topological Anderson insulating phase in multiple parameter ranges. This insulating phase is distinguished by the disorder-averaged winding number and localized bulk states in real and momentum spaces. Our research demonstrates that the topological phase boundaries match those predicted by the self-consistent Born approach, while also analyzing the impact of binary disorders on topological surface states and the topological Anderson phases. Additionally, we demonstrate that this phase can be triggered by simulated correlated disorders, revealing that the topological characteristics and localization lengths depend on the disorder correlation length and scale.

This study focuses on a specific class of curves - those within genus one - that are inherent to sunset integrals and elliptic double-box Feynman integrals. Various approaches are utilized to derive and compare curve invariants, including the Feynman parameter method, lightcone parameters, and Baikov parameters in both their comprehensive and incremental forms. Our analysis reveals equivalence among all computed invariants, thereby validating each method's capability to preserve curve structure. As an additional benefit, we generate and validate local Spence functions for the curve's invariant, which is crucial for the rigorous proof of finiteness found in the second step of the incremental approach.

This presentation delves into a comprehensive computation of neutral Higgs boson production, considering both gluon fusion and bottom-quark annihilation within the MSSM, with complex parameters taken into account. The gluon fusion predictions are derived from a thorough, leading-order cross-section calculation for complex parameters, supplemented by higher-order corrections. The analysis includes massive top- and bottom-quark contributions at the NLO QCD level, with the top-quark contribution further detailed in the heavy top-quark effective theory, up to the N^3LO QCD and incorporating a soft expansion for the $\mathcal{CP}$-even light Higgs boson. The calculations for the $\mathcal{CP}$-odd component of the light Higgs boson and the heavy Higgs bosons were conducted up to the NNLO QCD level. The study also considers two-loop electroweak effects, supersymmetric contributions within the heavy top-quark effective theory, and demonstrates the impact of the $\mathcal{CP}$-odd/tune even mixing at both the NLO QCD level for the light Higgs boson and at the leading order for the heavy Higgs bosons. The predictions for the effective couplings, $f_g$ and $f_\gamma$, squared, were obtained with the consideration of phase angles. The relevant code implementations, MH@NLO, MH@NNLO, and MSHRAC, were utilized in these calculations. A note is made that

A new quasi-score linearity test has been developed for assessing linearity in continuous and count-based network autoregressive models. The test's asymptotic distribution is analyzed under various scenarios, including fixed and increasing network dimensions, null hypotheses, and specific alternative hypotheses. Key findings indicate that when model parameters are identifiable, the test's distribution converges to the chi-square and noncentral chi-square forms. Notably, the results are robust to parameters at their space boundaries. For non-identifiable parameters, an alternative test has been proposed, along with an established asymptotic distribution for a fixed network dimension. Given the challenges of tabulating test critical values, an empirical approach is implemented for p-value calculation. This includes the use of feasible bounds and bootstrap approximations. The theoretical framework is supported by consistency and asymptotic normality findings for the quasi maximum likelihood estimator, under specific conditions. To illustrate the test's practical application, simulation results and a real-world p-value estimation based on a bootstrapped sample are provided, along with an implementation in the 'psm' R package.

Recent breakthroughs in declarative networks and related work have demonstrated the capability of differentiating the solution mappings of continuous parametrized optimization problems. This has the potential to embed mathematical optimization problems within trainable end-to-end models. By providing an alternative expression for computing derivatives, this differentiability enables significant reductions in memory requirements, obviating the need for unrolling optimization procedures during backward passes. However, this typically requires the computationally expensive inversion of large Hessian matrices. In this research, we examine two specific applications - robust vector pooling and optimal transport - to illustrate how problem structures can be leveraged to achieve more efficient computations during backward passes, reducing both memory and processing requirements. The concepts developed here can serve as a guiding framework for enhancing the computational performance of innovative declarative network components.

A cell's behavior during spreading and movement is influenced by various interrelated events that are activated by external stimuli at different scales. Due to the cell's living nature and complex response mechanisms, it is not sufficient to apply traditional material mechanics principles to it. Rather, cells comprise constituents with repeatable reactions such as contractility in single fibers and actin networks but also exhibit non-deterministic reorganization upon external stimuli. With consideration of this complexity, our goal is to develop a multi-faceted framework for modeling cellular spreading and movement, taking into account the movement of proteins across lipid membranes.

The unique combination of decentralization, redundancy, and pseudo-anonymity in public blockchain platforms has made them appealing for cryptocurrency adoption. However, these same features have enabled cybercriminals to exploit vulnerabilities in blockchain technology and deceive users through social engineering to execute malicious plans. Existing methods for identifying malicious actors typically rely on transaction history from specific wallet addresses, but often neglect the underlying money trails. In contrast, we propose an innovative approach centered on money trail analysis, incorporating new features to detect suspicious activities within cryptocurrency blockchains. Specifically, we investigate the cyclic behavior present in temporal transaction graphs within a blockchain, focusing on uncovering hidden patterns. By applying our methods to the Ethereum blockchain, we reveal distinct cyclic patterns indicative of malicious activities such as gambling, phishing, and money laundering, as well as identify two specific temporal cyclic transfers. Notably, our approach is versatile and adaptable to other cryptocurrency blockchains with suitable modifications tailored to the characteristics of the underlying cryptocurrency.

Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models.

Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. This can be accomplished through interferometry, by first manipulating highly entangled quantum states before collecting information about an unknown variable through single measurements. Although this typically yields the most effective outcome, applying this method is extremely difficult when dealing with larger states. Another approach is offered by quantum jump metrology, a method that extracts information by continuously monitoring the dynamics of individually tracked photons within metastable states. These systems develop correlations, known as multiple-photon entanglement, as a result of this measurement process, and precision can be increased proportionately. However, this method faces limitations in precision due to the unavoidable back-action of the measurement, which disrupts the desired state of sync. This difficulty can be overcome by utilizing a quantum non-demolition (QND) probe, which enables the extraction of information without disturbing the system in a way that affects the desired state of sync. This concept was previously demonstrated with a suitable model, which can also be physically realized with a couple of connected two-level systems that are interacting with a cavity, where the measurement of the photon number leads to the development of multi-photon entanglement. Furthermore, by analyzing this system with a real-world application in mind, such as optical clocks, it is possible to overcome the limitations of precision offered by conventional methods and approach a higher level of accuracy, which can be achieved through the use of a QND probe and thus leading to an increase in precision

The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data on $\pi^0$ $\pi^0$ correlation functions from Au$+$Au collisions at a root $s_{NN}$ of 200 GeV, 6.2 GeV, and 7.7 GeV, as well as $p$ $+$$p$ collisions at a root $s$ of 200 GeV and 7.7 GeV. The data shows hadrons exhibiting high-momentum fractions of their parent quarks in Au$+$Au collisions with $\pi^0$ jets, but this phenomenon is absent in $p$ $+$$p$ collisions. This observation supports the hypothesis of quasi-free hadron production within a colored medium, resulting in a $\pi^0$ jet with an associated hadronic cloud surrounding it. Hadrons at the periphery of this cloud may interfere with soft hadrons from the reaction, leading to an induction of narrow hadron resonances, or Chiral Magnetic Wave (CMW) effect. Data analysis also supports the existence of a CMW in $200$ GeV Au$+$Au collisions, consistent with chiral symmetry restoration near the phase diagram critical point.

This paper explores the behavior of Smarandache's sequence from the Online Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences (OEIS) at A061076, specifically focusing on its associated sequences, A061077 and A061078, linked to the Smarandache's sigma product of digits. We address open questions by identifying upper bounds applicable to all natural numbers 'n', as well as deriving closed formulas for sequences 'a(n)' and 'b(n)'. Our combined results provide insights into the behavior of the broader sequence 'c(n)'. To validate our findings, accompanying examples using Wolfram Mathematica scripts are included.

Cloud-based HPC deployments can provide cost savings and optimal resource allocation.
However, there are significant differences between the network architectures of cloud and on-premise HPC systems.
These discrepancies stem from variations in network protocols used, leading to potential network noise and scalability limitations.
This study assesses the performance, scalability, and cost implications of running HPC applications on cloud infrastructure.
Initially, the investigation focuses on latency, bandwidth, and data transfer patterns in small-scale tests, followed by simulations on larger systems.
Validation is conducted across multiple cloud providers and data centers, revealing that system latency and noise affect both performance and cost at small scale, whereas variability and data transfer patterns dominate forces at larger systems.
These findings indicate that the performance and behavior of distributed memory systems can diverge substantially between cloud and on-premise HPC setups.

Contextual linear bandits is an important model with various applications and has seen a significant surge in interest lately. This surge particularly occurred in the realm of wireless applications, where communication constraints pose a significant performance obstacle. Especially in scenarios where context dimensions are substantial. As a result, decentralized learning algorithms without信息共享 of context have experienced increased interest. We build on this area and investigate a memoryless contextual linear bandit learning algorithm without data信息共享. The context here is assumed to be generated independently at each agent. This algorithm achieves nearly optimal performance, significantly outperforming existing bounds by a factor of up to O(d) with just around 5d bits per context. Additionally, for context dimensions of up to around 200, our results indicate a potential for substantial performance improvement over centralized learning.

Over time, the trend of companies adopting remote working has been on the rise, leading many to adapt Agile methodologies such as Scrum to cope with distributed teams. However, the global shift to fully remote working brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic was a unprecedented phenomenon. This research involves a two-phase, multi-method approach. Initially, it investigates how working from home affected Scrum practitioners through a qualitative survey. Subsequently, it proposes and empirically tests a theoretical framework using PLS-SEM with data from a sample of 200 software engineers who experienced both remote and non-remote working periods. Our results demonstrate that well-supported basic psychological needs from home working enable more effective Scrum adoption than home working in isolation. Furthermore, integrating Scrum into the home working setup contributes to increased job performance. To facilitate better support for employees' psychological needs while working remotely, we propose that virtual team-building activities should be integrated into Scrum practices.

Our study investigates outcomes of the Event Shape Engineering method implemented in lead-lead collisions at a 2.76 TeV collision energy.  Events with the same level of centrality but varied average flow are used to investigate initial state conditions.  Results reveal that the event-shape selection's influence on the elliptic flow coefficient is unaffected by transverse momentum.  Also found is that charged hadron distributions are steeper for events exhibiting higher-than-average elliptic flow, indicating interactions between radial and elliptic flow phenomena.

This paper proposes the Quaternion Linear Canonical Stockwell Transform as a derivative of the Linear Canonical Transform, and proves related inequalities, including Heisenberg's Inequality and a logarithmic inequality for LCST.

This work utilizes the concepts from Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) analyses and extremal network theory to examine the extremal gain resulting from optimal power control in contrast to binary (on/off) power control in large interference networks, focusing on uncovering new theoretical insights. Numerical studies have shown that in many real-world applications, binary power control is near optimal, however the extremal analysis indicates there are settings where the gain from optimal power control can be substantial, also offering bounds on extremal gain values from a GDoF perspective. As its primary contribution, this research precisely defines the extremal GDoF gain of optimal over binary power control as proportional to $\sqrt{K}$, where $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ represents the ratio, for any network with $K$ components, further, it provides an attainable lower bound that confirms this finding. The proportionality constant from this bound has been determined to be at least $1/2\sqrt{2\pi}$, and the associated steady-state error power from these analyses is shown to be negligible, thus confirming the reliability of these results.

This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps, which distorts the simulation's representation of particle stretching and strain. Our multiple-time-step approach utilizes distinct time steps for simulating fluid flow and particle collisions while maintaining consistent equilibrium conditions for particles across these time steps. Our findings show that accurately modeling particle collisions requires capturing the full range of collision durations and velocities. As such, we demonstrate the inefficacy of model approaches that artificially alter collision time steps. Nevertheless, our method successfully captures particle clustering and sediment entrainment by correctly representing collision durations and velocities. Although simplifying the resolution of collisions leads to underestimating the transfer of kinetic energy, our method successfully maintains this balance and improves consistency in comparing simulations with different levels of collision resolution, thereby accurately modeling the impact of collisions on turbulence.

This article presents $2$ distinct proof methodologies establishing the existence of pairs of relatively prime positive integers, $a$ and $b$, for which the following congruence is satisfied: the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ can be factored as $7$ raised to a power of $n$.

A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot, specifically the Light-IIs model from Shanghai Tech, which uses thrust generators for lift and adhesion for securing its foot. By creating an experimental setup and a dynamic model of the robot and deformable soil, this research explores the capabilities and limitations of a simple control algorithm in facilitating efficient locomotion. The findings from this project offer insights into the effectiveness and boundaries of this approach, thus contributing to the field of legged locomotion research.

In this paper, the contact interaction model is applied to a specific class of two-body equations known as the Bernhardt-Heisenberg variational approach to produce adjusted masses for quarks, mesons, and their combined spectra. The mass calculations of the quarks and mesons are derived using specific vacuum expectation values, a particular set of wave functions, and an extensive numerical calculation technique called the Gauss-Laguerre integration.

Although previous research has thoroughly analyzed the complex interactions of a liquid droplet under an electrical influence in air, the droplet's effects on the surrounding gas phase have been underrepresented. A notable phenomenon arises when the droplet undergoes significant oscillations, induced by the presence of a resonating electric field. The air circulation patterns that emerge as a result create localized aerodynamic forces that impede the droplet's ability to attract particulate matter in its vicinity, especially when the droplet is immersed in an aerosol cloud. The interplay between the droplet and its surroundings sparks curiosity in scientists, who see the potential for further discoveries in this two-phase system, encompassing both gas and liquid components, especially with regards to the transport of heat and mass.

Effective communication through language cannot be fully achieved without considering negation, a fundamental aspect of all human languages. Despite being present in every language, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering English reading comprehension dataset. It demands that models infer the implications of negated statements within passages, collected from a diverse set of paragraphs featuring varied negation cues. Additionally, human evaluators asked questions about the passages, some incorporating the negations, while others did not. Notably, the answers to these paired questions should be contrary, thereby ensuring a thorough assessment of model performance. Unlike other reading comprehension datasets, CONDAQA does not rely on irrelevant distruter sentences to increase difficulty, offering a more rigorous benchmark for NLP models. Our findings indicate that prominent BERT-based models without specific negation knowledge struggle to tackle CONDAQA, while those equipped with explicit negation cues or world knowledge can answer the questions, highlighting the difficulty of this dataset. Furthermore, we examine how NLP models process semantically varied negation cues, leading to the discovery that such variations impact model answers. CONDAQA serves as a crucial stepping stone towards improving NLP systems that can handle negation, ultimately contributing to more robust language understanding.

Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques limit themselves to hierarchical structures based solely on pre-selected key elements, resulting in a loss of contextual relationships. To address this limitation, we propose a novel, context-aware approach that derives an information hierarchy from the unique characteristics of web pages, utilizing a model that treats each page as a context-dependent component within a broader network. Our context-based hierarchy model is further refined by incorporating the network effects of neighboring pages, allowing for the creation of flexible organizational structures. These structures can be viewed as part of a larger, interconnected network, rather than separate components, and our method enables the context-aware navigation of web search results, providing users with a more intuitive and effective user experience. Our method also enables the context-aware navigation of intranets, allowing users to navigate more intuitively and effectively.

Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the tunneling gap in quantum annealing dictates both the divergence between the quenched state and the ground state following a quench, as well as both the fidelity and dynamical observables' behavior post-quench. Notably, when the gap reaches a certain low magnitude, both delicate tunneling and overplayed quenching occur, providing a unique duality between quantum annealing and quenching. This relationship is examined across diverse, intricate models, including the Ising model with random, diagonal interactions, and the phase diagram of known and independently developed minimal gaps in relation to both fidelity and quench outcomes. Consequently, this work establishes a direct correlation between the performance of quantum annealing and quenching, offering a theoretical basis for optimizing quenching protocols based on annealing dynamics and vice versa.

Conformance checking focuses on comparing modeled process behavior to observed process behavior from actual event data. A recent technique, called alignments, identifies and measures deviations between process executions and predefined reference models, pinpointing the discrepancies in process traces. Notably, alignments require entire or initial segments of process runs from start to finish; this paper explores new methods to analyze partial process runs and assesses these methods with real-world event data.

Starting from a reliable two-dimensional model with two bands derived from
$d$ and $s$ orbital types for infinite layered nickelates, we investigate the
extent to which it can be reduced to a simplified one-band Hubbard model. 
Screening of the $s$-like orbital's influence is a critical factor here. 
Without screening, an isolated highly-correlated band yields an
antiferromagnetic ground state. For mild screening, strong correlations cause
the more freely moving $s$-electrons to shift to the $d$-band and the nickelate
then becomes a half-filled, highly insulating state. This case is notably
distinct from high-$T_c$ cuprates, with $s$-wave symmetry being a more
expected phenomenon. 
On the other hand, strong screening leads to a mixture of filled and weakly
coupled $s$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ bands and results in self-doped $d$ orbital and
$d$-wave pairing tendencies emerging. 
Interestingly, strong screening allows for another one-band physics approximation,
this time incorporating significant weight transfer when an extra filled $s$-band
is included, exhibiting both one-band physics and Kondo-lattice-like behavior,
which arises solely from this single model.

This paper examines the long-term behavior of the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation under weak collisions in an infinite space near a global equilibrium, specifically focusing on soft potentials. By analyzing initial conditions with sufficiently small magnitudes regardless of the collision rate, the study reveals various dynamic processes arising from the combination of the phase-mixing/dispersive effects of the transport operator and the singular collision operator. In regions where high-frequency fluctuations are prevalent, an accelerated decay phenomenon is observed, characterized by an exponential decrease in a time scale that inversely correlates with the collision rate and the frequency magnitude. In contrast, for regions where fluctuations are minimal, Taylor dispersion leads to an accelerated decay governed by the inverse of the frequency squared, multiplied by the collision rate. These diverse decay patterns enable us to establish equivalent bounds for solution norms in various function spaces, influencing the dispersion and decay properties of the resulting measure.

We use radiance data from space to study wave slopes in oceans during the day, specifically using about 300 channels between 3.6 and 4.0 $\mu$m, which takes into account solar radiation reflected off the water. This approach uses a large dataset of around 150 million observations, enabling the derivation of wind-speed dependent wave-slope probabilities up to 15 m/s. Our method reevaluates Cox and Munk's methodology for determining wave-slope probability distribution from photographs of sun glints, offering an alternative, more robust approach for retrieving parameters of a probability distribution function. Our results for wave slope statistics are comparable to previous findings, yet our data exhibits reduced uncertainties, particularly in higher-order moments, and indicates an asymmetric wave slope distribution that's consistent with observations and simulations.

When designing a software system, a modification in one component may
unintentionally impact other parts, hindering overall system performance. This is
addressed by conducting regression testing, which re-evaluates system sections
aimed at preventing adverse effects. However, pinpointing these affected areas
proves challenging, making it essential to identify system changes through a
different approach. We apply singular value decomposition to group software
modifications by their functional roles, allowing for more efficient detection
of areas requiring retesting during subsequent updates. By leveraging parallel
calculations on shared memory systems, we enhance testing speed, ensuring optimal
results can be obtained even as software systems scale up.

The COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread disruption, with numerous countries enforcing strict lockdowns and millions of lives affected. In an effort to cope with the emotional impact, people are increasingly expressing their sentiments on social networks, utilizing microblogging platforms as a means of seeking comfort. Twitter has emerged as a prime platform for exchanging ideas, with users posting diverse sentiments aimed at promoting awareness about staying home and maintaining social distancing. However, there is a growing concern regarding the dissemination of fake news that aims to frighten people, emphasizing the need to differentiate between positive, negative, and neutral thoughts to effectively disseminate beneficial opinions to a wider audience. Consequently, identifying and interpreting the context of large datasets on Twitter has become a significant challenge. In this paper, a comprehensive analysis of Twitter data using various machine learning algorithms was conducted to evaluate sentiment, and subsequent context learning of the dataset based on sentiment was explored, revealing a direct correlation between complex data patterns and simplified sentimental data.

Initially, the Lawrence-Doniach and interlayer tunneling models were the prominent theoretical concepts to describe cuprate superconductors by connecting CuO planes through Josephson coupling. Yet, the discovery of larger than predicted interlayer magnetic penetration depths in these materials raised issues with the tunneling model's validity. The emergence of planar stripes and charge domains enabled alternative Josephson coupling theories. Our study finds the average intralayer interaction to be greater than interlayer coupling and comparable to condensation energy, ultimately yielding long-range phase order-driven superconductivity. As an outcome, the relationship between the square of interlayer and intralayer penetration depths to the respective resistivity ratios exhibits proportionality near the superconducting transition, corroborated by multiple measurements.

The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars, are intriguingly ambiguous and may influence neutron star dynamics as detected via gravitational waves.  As a compact star's density increases, sound velocity approaches the conformal limit at high densities, satisfying the causality limit while its detailed behavior remains disputed. It's hypothesized that dense matter sound velocity can be an indicator of a deconfinement phase transition, possibly exhibiting a distinctive relationship with density. Our work delves into the fundamental properties of dense matter sound velocity and the adiabatic index within neutron stars, quark stars, and hybrid stars.  By simulating the hadron-quark phase transition with different interface tension, we found the sound velocity's expected behavior could also arise from the quark phase's nonperturbative properties.  Consequently, this could result in a denser star with similar mass, thus providing the groundwork for a new type of quark star equation of states that may be tested through high-precision pulsar radius measurements.

The established Tai mapping between two trees $T_1$ and $T_2$ is a unique one-to-one correlation of their nodes that maintains the ancestral hierarchy. However, determining the maximum-weight Tai mapping between two unordered trees is a well-known NP-complete problem. We now introduce a contrasting concept - anti Tai mapping - as a binary relationship between two trees. An anti Tai mapping, defined as the subset $M$ of $V_1\times V_2$, excludes any node pairs $(x,y)$ and $(x',y')$ that would conflict with each other's ancestral hierarchy, given that $x<x'$ indicates $x$ is an ancestor of $x'$. Calculating the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping plays a significant role in solving the maximum-weight Tai mapping problem through integer programming by applying the cutting plane method. We provide an efficient algorithm for computing a maximum-weight anti Tai mapping when one tree is a path. Additionally, we show that by applying a restricted version of anti Tai mapping, where nodes sharing the same path as their ancestors must not correspond, we can obtain a polynomially computable lower bound for the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping between any two trees. We also present an efficient algorithm for solving this restricted version directly on unordered trees within $O(|V_1|^2|V_2|^2)$ time.

We investigate a variety of non-classical states made up of superposed, both squeezed and displaced number states, examining their phase space structure in relation to Heisenberg limited sensitivity in parameter estimation. Certain combinations of these states exhibit minimal uncertainty, while others display increased curvature in their trajectories, indicating potential for enhanced estimation accuracy. Notably, some of these non-classical states include previously studied states such as the cat phase state and the Schrödinger cat state, as well as other states such as the phase kick state and the cat-like state. Our research identifies optimal local measurements that yield distinct interference patterns, providing a pathway for distinguishing these states experimentally.

A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems, which can generate the thermal energy needed to create and destroy small particles, potentially influencing where these particles grow or break apart.  Although the VSI has been thoroughly studied, its effects on larger, solid objects such as planets and moons, and the accumulation of ring-like structures, are not fully understood.  This research aims to understand how the growth of dust particles affects the VSI, drawing on a new, comprehensive model that considers the interaction between the gas and solid components of planets, moon rings, and ring-like structures in solid objects within the Thompson Disc Model.  It finds that in areas of the VSI where dust growth is prominent, the growth rate of the instability is significantly slowed, and may not persist for an extended period of time.  It also identifies regions within protoplanetary disks where the dust growth is insufficient to suppress the VSI, and as dust grows over time, it could both quench and restart the instability, depending on the stage of the disk's development.  This dynamic may provide a framework for identifying and locating sites of planet formation within the disk, or even serve as a trigger for the formation of planets.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional.

Recent advancements in outsourcing training and machine learning as a service have created innovative threats such as hidden functionalities that are embedded in artificial neural networks. In typical research scenarios, triggers that activate these embedded features are static in their positioning, pixel values, and detection mechanisms, making them relatively easy to detect and secure against retraining. However, dynamic triggers that activate based on input images or artificial neural network parameters, are significantly more challenging to defend against, particularly over multiple training sessions. This research explores the threat landscape of machine learning as a service, focusing on a particular scenario called remote learning, in which the adversary controls both the learning process and the data generation process. We introduce three novel dynamic backdoors called sleeping, dreaming, and waking backdoors, and demonstrate that they can be implemented with remarkable efficiency and difficulty to detect, even when employing state-of-the-art detection methods. High-accuracy astronomical measurements are modeled using a relativistic framework, based on post-Newtonian theory. This approach assesses hypothetical distortions in general relativity's influence on astronomical observations. A key factor influencing these measurements is a post-Newtonian parameter, denoted by $\gamma$, which determines how much light is shifted due to the movement of sources. By utilizing the LASP satellite data from 2017, which tracked the position of the Moon relative to the Satellite Stabilization Platform over nearly a year, a study was able to estimate the effect of parallax on these measurements. It was determined that under this setup, a deviation in $\gamma$ from one unit can significantly impact parallax estimations, particularly when the parallax angle is large. However, it was also found that systems lacking parallax movement, such as Satellite Stabilization Platforms, are less susceptible to errors in $\gamma$ and can serve as useful references for detecting such deviations at a distant scale. Ultimately, this study demonstrates the importance of accounting for relativistic effects in high-precision astrometry and explores the potential of satellite astrometry in identifying discrepancies in $\gamma$ based on current and future missions.

We have developed an efficient approach for condensing complex systems into their fundamental behaviors using their primary underlying features. By leveraging observed data, we pinpoint a low-dimensional structure that characterizes the systems' gradual evolution and generate an extremely simple representation of the systems' dynamics within that structure. Building on the SSMLearn algorithm, which applies implicit optimization to identify this structure, we can create a highly streamlined system that captures the essential dynamics. This results in a dramatically simplified model with at most as many variables as time-series sequences and at most one new parameter for each dimension in the structure, making it possible to achieve an exceptionally efficient dynamics model.

Certain fundamental models which result in one- and two-dimensional solitons, like those for Bose-Einstein condensates described by the Gross-Pitaevskii equations, have the property of Galilean invariance. This allows for solitons to be moved from a stationary state by incorporating invariance. Researchers face a challenge in finding models capable of exhibiting stable, self-accelerating motion of solitons. Self-accelerating modes are well-documented in linear systems in the form of waves. A combination of solitons and self-accelerating modes would have significant applications in areas such as precision measurements, optical trapping, and controlled propagation of matter waves. A pair of coupled, chemically identical Bose-Einstein condensates can potentially provide the necessary conditions, as long as their interaction with the condensate is balanced. A specific model consisting of three coupled equations is derived from this perspective, and it is shown to have stationary solutions in its form, and these solutions can be transformed into moving forms through the application of Galilean invariance transformations.

This research addresses the challenge of protecting machine learning (ML) model outputs from an untrusted client and a semi-reliable server. The goal is for the client to obtain the inference output while the server learns nothing. Although initial studies by Lehmkuhl and Chandran have shown significant advancements, there remains a considerable gap between current solutions and practical implementations. To address this issue, our proposal SIMC 2.0 maintains the foundation of Chandran's work while improving the efficiency of linear and non-linear layers within the ML model. Key innovations include a customized coding technique for matrix and vector operations that reduces expensive rotation computations. Furthermore, SIMC 2.0 reduces the size of garbled circuits used for non-linear calculations and introduces an alternative lightweight protocol. As a result, our experiments demonstrate substantial performance gains for linear computations (up to 17 times faster), reduced computation and communication in non-linear layers (by at least 4 times), and enhanced overall runtime for ML model inference.

Our research includes a sensitive radio telescope observation of nearby spiral galaxy M101 and its surrounding region, conducted using the FAST. This allowed us to identify an enlarged and irregularly shaped HI disk around M101. Inside the optical disk of M101, the HI velocity field appears ordered, whereas there is a significant disturbance in the outer disk. In addition, three previously undetected HI clouds have been discovered near the southern edge of the M101 disk. These HI clouds have estimated masses of 1.3$\times$10$^{7}$ $M_{\odot}$, 2.4$\times$10$^{7}$ $M_{\odot}$, and 2.0$\times$10$^{7}$ $M_{\odot}$ respectively. The largest of these HI clouds exhibits an internal structure similar to a galaxy's rotated interior. Our findings indicate a possible explanation for these HI clouds - they may be the result of interactions between M101 and its satellite dSph galaxy NGC 3190. These interactions could also provide a possible origin for the HI clouds and the extra HI observed around M101.

To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common to incorporate external knowledge. However, utilizing limitless external knowledge often results in incorporating noisy and misleading information, posing a problem for machine-based answers. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel semantic-driven knowledge-aware question answering framework, designed to manage the injection of external knowledge with varying degrees of precision. Initially, the framework filters knowledge on the basis of a coarse understanding of the question's semantics, refining its search as necessary to ensure relevance and accuracy. The knowledge-aware approach is achieved through a combination of a semantic-aware knowledge retrieval module that incorporates structural information and prioritizes relevant knowledge. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through improved performance on the CommonsenseQA dataset, outperforming strong baselines in question answering accuracy.

Astronomical environments, particularly in comets, are rich in molecular cations whose exceptional brightness under UV to visible light can facilitate the understanding of local plasma environments and the composition of cometary neutral gas. Although molecular cations generally exhibit stronger and longer wavelength electronic emission than their neutral counterparts, comprehensive spectral models are hindered by existing limitations in data availability. For the most straightforward species, including oxygen-based molecules such as water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and hydroxyl, there are significant gaps in spectral reference data in some frequency ranges. As a result, cometary spectral modeling based on these species is currently incomplete. This study utilizes the smFAB method to model several cometary planar cations, such as H2O+, CO2+, OH+, and MAG+ (where MAG represents a generic molecule), in order to demonstrate the capability of this technique in cometary spectral modeling. By doing so, it also highlights the necessity for an expanded range of cometary gas neutral species to be made ionized and investigated in a laboratory setting.

The challenge of representing a positive entity as a sum of squared components dates back centuries to notable mathematicians Bachet and Lagrange. Though successful methods exist for certain types of structures (such as integers or polynomial equations with rational coefficients), the task remains an open question for numerous other fundamental structures and fields. In this study, we introduce a direct procedure for dividing any element of a global domain (either a number domain or a global function domain) into the sum of the minimal-length squared components.

Our team employed photonic technology to revolutionize the conventional method of spectroscopy, enabling on-device spectral cross-correlation using a template spectrum. This was achieved by designing photonic devices with intricately modulated transmission spectra, thus performing cross-correlation without the need for dispersion. Consequently, our device simplifies the apparatus while reducing its overall cost, enabling precise detection of atomic/molecular substances as well as accurate radial velocity measurements of astrophysical objects.

We outline two innovative design approaches based on distinct photonic platforms, silicon and fibre-based photonics. Silicon-based photonic technology incorporates thermally modulated ring resonators for spectral cross-correlation, whereas fibre-based photonics utilize strain-modulated customized fibre Bragg gratings. Both approaches successfully detected molecular gas in a laboratory setting and are currently undergoing field testing.

Furthermore, our research has far-reaching implications as these photonic devices may pave the way for developing low-cost, custom-built spectrographic instruments capable of simultaneously analyzing multiple objects or providing high-resolution field spectra. This technology has immense potential to contribute to groundbreaking research in stellar radial velocity measurements and exoplanet discoveries.

In the last few years, various machine learning models have emerged with the aim of tackling polypharmacy side effects, predicting medication interactions, and optimizing combination therapies. This paper takes a comprehensive approach, offering a theoretical framework that can address these challenges through relational machine learning models. It provides key concepts, assesses existing model architectures, discusses relevant evaluation metrics, datasets, and testing protocols, and suggests K-shot learning as a effective method for evaluating the generalizability of these models to new patient data. Finally, it discusses significant implications of this work, including the potential for relational machine learning to lead to omissions, errors, or inaccuracies in reasoning about therapeutic decisions.

The provided article introduces an Itô-Wentzell type formula tailored to accommodate paths with α-Hölder regularity of $\alpha$ within the interval $(\frac{1}{3}, \frac{1}{2}]$. Additionally, it expands on prior work by R. Castrequini and P. Catuogno concerning Young integrals, as well as research by C. Keller and J. Zhang on rough paths.

In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server, often exacerbated by the heterogeneous distribution of data. This issue is particularly pronounced in settings where nodes have limited computing power, such as in the Internet of Things. A possible solution involves utilizing innovative protocols that enable peer-to-peer communication, allowing nodes to exchange model updates with their neighboring neighbors. This paper evaluates such an approach in the context of Federated Learning and demonstrates its effectiveness in reducing communication requirements compared to traditional methods. It also explores the development of theoretical convergence bounds for this approach, providing guarantees regarding its ability to achieve an optimal solution within a given communication budget.

Three-dimensional rotating turbulence, once believed to be dominated by stable geostrophic vortices, has recently been observed to support highly dynamic, downscale energy cascades. In a recent study, researchers employed direct numerical simulations within a triply periodic box, artificially suppressing geostrophic vortices to investigate the properties of turbulent flows. These simulations revealed an inertial wave turbulence that conforms to a specific spectrum first described analytically by Galtier in 2003. Interestingly, it was found that the same underlying mechanisms could either give rise to wave turbulence or stable geostrophic vortices depending solely on the initial conditions, thus further establishing the concept of bi-stability in rotating turbulent flows.

Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the likelihood of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 to 24 percent and reduced it over a ten-year time frame by 7 percent.  The data also indicated that mental health treatment treatment had no measurable impact on violent crimes but did reduce property crimes and other non-violent offenses.  An additional analysis suggested an increase in quality of life for treated individuals, as reflected in higher life satisfaction scores.

A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique, combining interpolation methods to enhance semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The proposed strategy uses consistency regularization to ensure the segmentation of mixed data matches the mixed segmentations. This approach belongs to the category of adaptive data regularization techniques that reduce overfitting when working with highly confident labelled data. The method has several advantages over alternative techniques such as adversarial and generative models, primarily due to its minimal computational requirements. Evaluations using publicly available MRI datasets - specifically ACDC and MMWHS - demonstrate that this proposed technique outperforms existing semi-supervised models, with source code available on GitHub.

To handle increased luminosity at the Large Hadron Collider in 2021, the ATLAS collaboration will undertake a major upgrade to the LHC's detector system. This enhancement includes upgrading the Level 1 trigger based on calorimeter data to utilize finer details of the data, courtesy of the Feature EXtractors (FEX) system. Specifically, the jet FEX (jFEX) system aims to enhance jet identification and calculate global variables within an extremely tight latency constraint of under 400 nanoseconds. This will involve six distinct modules, where each module on an ATCA board contains four high-end Xilinx FPGAs to process the data at an astonishing 3.6 terabytes per second rate. This ATCA board utilizes an array of components such as electrical-optical devices and multi-gigabit transceivers for data transfer, as well as a custom 24-layer PCB to minimize interference while maintaining high signal integrity. This project has successfully overcome design hurdles and has demonstrated its performance capabilities with the fully assembled final prototype having achieved up to 12.8 gigabits per second during in-house and CERN integrated testing. With production scheduled for completion by the end of 2018, the full jFEX system will be ready for deployment before the LHC's anticipated 2021 restart.

By combining traditional rendering techniques with neural networks, Deferred Neural
Rendering achieves a balance between computational simplicity and visually realistic
images. Extending DNR to use skinned meshes for rendering dynamic objects would
significantly expand its potential applications. However, doing so requires accounting
for unmodeled mesh deformations and potential misalignments, which can otherwise
jeopardize the rendering pipeline. To address these challenges for realistic virtual
human avatars, we developed Articulated Neural Rendering, a new framework that
extends DNR. In experiments and user evaluations, ANR consistently outperformed not
only DNR but also other avatar creation methods, demonstrating its superiority
through clear preferences and outstanding results on quantitative assessment metrics.
ANR enabled significantly improved visual stability, level of detail, and overall
plausibility in both static and dynamic scenes.

To gain a deeper understanding of the performance and lifespan of materials, 
it's crucial to assess their atomic disorder levels. To this end, we use a unique
approach that leverages graph neural networks to create an interpretable disorder 
metric, effectively capturing local atomic configuration variability across the
solid to liquid phase spectrum. This methodical approach is tested with three
models featuring different disorder levels, including interfaces between solid 
and liquid phases, multi-crystalline microstructures, and grain boundaries, 
using elemental aluminum as a prime example. Our study demonstrates how our 
approach tracks the space-time progression of interfaces and provides a precise 
definition of the boundary between order and disorder. Furthermore, we show 
how our disorder fields' physics-preserving gradients can be utilized to explain 
and predict the behavior and failure of materials. Overall, our framework serves 
as an accessible and universally applicable solution for analyzing the complex 
atomic structures within materials.

Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying factors behind their success remain poorly understood. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. These inconsistencies hinder real-world applicability in educational settings.
